children.title: Rotated Quadratic-Cone Barriers
children.top_down_role: Barrier geometry for rotated second-order cone representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotated Quadratic-Cone Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical barrier obtained by linear equivalence with a Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge 1\), define the rotated quadratic cone \(Q_d^r=\{(u,v,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d:u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\lVert x\rVert_2^2\}\). On its interior, define \[F_r(u,v,x)=-\log\!\left(2uv-\lVert x\rVert_2^2\right).\] The invertible transformation \(T(u,v,x)=(u+v,u-v,\sqrt2x)\) maps \(Q_d^r\) onto the Lorentz cone \(L_{d+2}\), and the Lorentz quadratic form of \(T(u,v,x)\) equals \[ (u+v)^2-(u-v)^2-2\lVert x\rVert_2^2=2\left(2uv-\lVert x\rVert_2^2\right). \] Thus the pulled-back Lorentz barrier differs from \(F_r\) only by the constant \(-\log 2\). Consequently, \(F_r\) is a \(2\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier and satisfies \(F_r(\alpha u,\alpha v,\alpha x)=F_r(u,v,x)-2\log\alpha\) for every \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rotated quadratic cone is linearly equivalent to a Lorentz cone. The Lorentz quadratic form becomes twice the rotated quadratic slack, so negative log slack is a parameter-two barrier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_r\) is a \(2\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier for \(Q_d^r\).

notation.meaning: linear isomorphism from the rotated quadratic cone to the Lorentz cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Native-coordinate self-duality map and conjugate of the rotated quadratic barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(u,v,x)=2uv-\|x\|_2^2\) and \(F_r=-\log q\). Then \[-\nabla F_r(u,v,x)=\frac{(2v,2u,-2x)}{q(u,v,x)}\] maps \(\operatorname{int}Q_d^r\) bijectively onto itself and is involutive. The Fenchel conjugate is finite exactly on \(-\operatorname{int}Q_d^r\), where \[F_r^*(y)=-2+\log4-\log q(y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative gradient of the rotated-cone barrier is an involutive self-duality map, and its conjugate has the same logarithmic form up to a constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: -\nabla F_r:\operatorname{int}Q_d^r\to\operatorname{int}Q_d^r\text{ is involutive, and }\operatorname{dom}F_r^*=-\operatorname{int}Q_d^r.

children.top_down_role: Cone symmetries relevant to intrinsic barrier geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone Preservation Does Not Mean Exact Quadratic-Form Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary distinction between Lorentz-cone automorphisms and exact Lorentz isometries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(c>0\), the dilation \(A=cI\) satisfies \(A L_{d+1}=L_{d+1}\), but \[A^TJA=c^2J.\] Thus it preserves the Lorentz quadratic form exactly only when \(c=1\), while the canonical barrier transforms as \[F_L(Az)=F_L(z)-2\log c.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive dilations are cone automorphisms but generally scale, rather than exactly preserve, the Lorentz quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: cI\in\operatorname{Aut}(L_{d+1}),\qquad (cI)^TJ(cI)=c^2J.

notation.meaning: matrix of the Lorentz quadratic form

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Preservation Does Not Mean Exact Quadratic-Form Preservation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization and Transitivity of Lorentz-Cone Automorphisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conformal characterization, barrier covariance, generators, transitivity, and low-dimensional qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_n=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n-1}:t\ge\|x\|_2\}\) and \(J=\operatorname{diag}(1,-I_{n-1})\). For \(n\ge3\), \[A\in\operatorname{Aut}(L_n)\iff A^TJA=\lambda J\text{ for some }\lambda>0\text{ and }Ae_0\in\operatorname{int}L_n.\] Equivalently, these automorphisms are generated by positive dilations, spatial orthogonal maps, and time-orientation-preserving Lorentz boosts. They act transitively on \(\operatorname{int}L_n\), and the canonical barrier satisfies \[F_L(Az)=F_L(z)-\log\lambda.\] For \(n=1\), the automorphisms are positive scalings of a ray. For \(n=2\), null coordinates identify \(L_2\) with \(\mathbb R_+^2\), whose automorphisms are positive diagonal maps, possibly followed by coordinate exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lorentz-cone automorphisms are precisely the time-orientation-preserving conformal Lorentz transformations; they preserve barrier geometry up to an additive constant and act transitively on the interior.
assumptions_latex: The conformal characterization uses \(n\ge3\); the ray and two-dimensional cases are stated separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\in\operatorname{Aut}(L_n)\iff A^TJA=\lambda J\text{ and }Ae_0\in\operatorname{int}L_n,\quad F_L(Az)=F_L(z)-\log\lambda.

notation.meaning: matrix of the Lorentz quadratic form

knowledge_statements.title: Characterization and Transitivity of Lorentz-Cone Automorphisms
Second-Order Cone Automorphisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation law of the canonical barrier under Lorentz-cone automorphisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\ge2\), let \(J=\operatorname{diag}(1,-I_d)\), and let \(A\in\operatorname{GL}(d+1,\mathbb R)\) satisfy \(A L_{d+1}=L_{d+1}\). Then there exists \(\lambda>0\) such that \(A^TJA=\lambda J\). Hence, for \(z\in\operatorname{int}L_{d+1}\), the canonical barrier \(F_L(z)=-\log(z^TJz)\) obeys \[F_L(Az)=F_L(z)-\log\lambda.\] Thus every cone automorphism preserves the barrier’s gradient and Hessian geometry up to the corresponding linear change of coordinates, and the automorphism group acts transitively on \(\operatorname{int}L_{d+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lorentz-cone automorphisms scale the defining quadratic form, so the canonical barrier changes only by an additive constant and has invariant local geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^TJA=\lambda J\) for some \(\lambda>0\), and \(F_L(Az)=F_L(z)-\log\lambda\).

notation.meaning: matrix of the Lorentz quadratic form
group of invertible real linear maps

knowledge_statements.title: Nonradial Quadratic-Boundary Singularity
Degenerate Quadratic Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary singularities of Lorentz and rotated quadratic-cone barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Lorentz barrier, write \(s=t^2-\lVert x\rVert_2^2\); for the rotated-cone barrier, write \(s=2uv-\lVert x\rVert_2^2\). In either case the barrier is \(F=-\log s\) on \(s>0\). Along any interior sequence with \(s\downarrow0\), one has \(F\to+\infty\) and \(\lVert\nabla F\rVert\to+\infty\) unless the quadratic differential vanishes at the limit. At the cone apex the defining quadratic has zero gradient, but the barrier remains undefined and its Hessian has no finite extension. Boundary or apex points therefore cannot serve as ordinary Newton iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic-cone barriers become singular as quadratic slack vanishes; the apex does not admit a finite smooth extension and cannot initialize an interior Newton method.
assumptions_latex: The sequence remains in the interior of a Lorentz or rotated quadratic cone.
Its quadratic slack \(s\) converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\to+\infty\), and no finite twice-differentiable barrier extension exists at the degenerate boundary.

notation.meaning: negative logarithm of the quadratic slack

children.title: Positive-Semidefinite Log-Determinant Barriers
children.top_down_role: Spectral barriers for real, complex, and Hermitian semidefinite cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Log-Determinant Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical spectral barrier on real symmetric and complex Hermitian positive-semidefinite cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb H_n\) denote either the real vector space of real symmetric matrices or the real vector space of complex Hermitian matrices, and let \(\mathbb H_n^+=\{X\in\mathbb H_n:X\succeq0\}\). On \(\operatorname{int}\mathbb H_n^+=\{X:X\succ0\}\), define \[F(X)=-\log\det X=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log\lambda_i(X).\] This is an \(n\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier: \(F(\alpha X)=F(X)-n\log\alpha\) for \(\alpha>0\), and \(F(X_k)\to+\infty\) whenever positive-definite \(X_k\) approaches a singular positive-semidefinite matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative log determinant is the canonical rank-n spectral barrier for real symmetric or complex Hermitian positive-semidefinite matrices.
assumptions_latex: The complex Hermitian space is regarded as a real Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(X)=-\log\det X\) is an \(n\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier for \(\mathbb H_n^+\).

notation.meaning: real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrix space

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Up to the constant minus n, the conjugate is negative log determinant on the negative-definite cone.

abla F_J(x)=-x^{-1},\qquad 
abla^2F_J(x)=P(x^{-1}),\qquad [

Jordan-Determinant Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Determinant barrier on a symmetric cone represented by a Euclidean Jordan algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\), let \(K=\{x\circ x:x\in V\}\), and let \(\det_J x\) be the product of the \(r\) eigenvalues in a Jordan spectral decomposition. On \(\operatorname{int}K\), define \[F_J(x)=-\log\det_J x.\] The Jordan determinant is positive on \(\operatorname{int}K\) and homogeneous of degree \(r\). Consequently, \(F_J(\alpha x)=F_J(x)-r\log\alpha\) for every \(\alpha>0\); moreover, \(F_J\) is the canonical \(r\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-scaled, hence self-concordant, barrier of the symmetric cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative logarithm of the Jordan determinant gives the canonical barrier of a symmetric cone, with parameter equal to the Jordan rank.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Irreducible Decomposition and Classification of Symmetric Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural decomposition of finite-dimensional symmetric cones and classification of their irreducible factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-dimensional nonzero symmetric cone is reducible exactly when its Euclidean Jordan algebra decomposes as a nontrivial orthogonal direct sum of Jordan ideals. Every symmetric cone decomposes as a finite direct product of irreducible symmetric cones, uniquely up to permutation and factor isomorphism. Each irreducible factor is isomorphic to a real, complex, or quaternionic Hermitian positive-semidefinite cone, a Lorentz cone, or the exceptional cone \(H_3(\mathbb O)_+\), subject to the standard low-dimensional coincidences among presentations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric-cone reducibility is equivalent to Jordan-ideal decomposition; every symmetric cone has a unique product decomposition into factors from the five irreducible families.
assumptions_latex: The cone and associated Euclidean Jordan algebra are finite-dimensional and nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\cong\prod_iK_i\text{ uniquely up to order and isomorphism, with each }K_i\text{ in a standard irreducible family}.
knowledge_statements.title: Irreducible Decomposition and Classification of Symmetric Cones
Reducible Symmetric Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-product reducibility of symmetric cones and their Euclidean Jordan algebras.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonzero symmetric cone \(K\) is reducible if there exist nonzero symmetric cones \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) and a linear isomorphism \(T\) such that \(T(K)=K_1\times K_2\). Equivalently, for the Euclidean Jordan algebra \(V\) associated with \(K\), there is a nontrivial orthogonal direct-sum decomposition \(V=V_1\oplus V_2\) into Jordan ideals, with \(K=K_1\times K_2\) after identifying the factors. Iterating this decomposition expresses every symmetric cone as a finite product of irreducible symmetric cones, uniquely up to factor order and isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric cone is reducible exactly when its Jordan algebra splits into nonzero ideals, yielding a direct product of smaller symmetric cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional nonzero symmetric cone.
\(V\) is its associated Euclidean Jordan algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is reducible exactly when \(K\cong K_1\times K_2\) with both factors nonzero.

notation.meaning: orthogonal direct sum of Jordan ideals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reducibility definition fits the leaf, but the Jordan-ideal equivalence and unique finite irreducible decomposition require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Cross-Factor Perturbation Can Destroy Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing that boundary blow-up and valid factor barriers do not control a coupled perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R_{++}^2\), define \[G_\varepsilon(x_1,x_2)=-\log x_1-\log x_2+\varepsilon\sin x_1\sin x_2,\qquad \varepsilon>0.\] The added term is bounded, so \(G_\varepsilon\to+\infty\) when either coordinate approaches zero. At points \(x_1=x_2=\pi/2+2\pi k\), its Hessian is diagonal with entries \(x_1^{-2}-\varepsilon\), which are negative for all sufficiently large \(k\). Thus \(G_\varepsilon\) is not convex and cannot be a self-concordant barrier on the product cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a bounded smooth cross-factor perturbation can preserve boundary blow-up while destroying global convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_\varepsilon\text{ diverges at the boundary but is nonconvex on }\mathbb R_{++}^2.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Cross-Factor Perturbation Can Destroy Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between cone-local barrier separability and global Newton-system coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\prod_iK_i\) and \(F(x)=\sum_iF_i(x_i)\), shared equations \(\sum_iA_ix_i=b\) do not alter the block-separable barrier derivatives, although the resulting KKT or Schur system generally couples the factor directions through the \(A_i\). By contrast, adding a nonseparable term to \(F\) changes its Hessian and requires a new global verification of convexity, boundary blow-up, and self-concordance; componentwise barrier validity supplies none of these conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine equations may couple factor directions without destroying a separable barrier, whereas coupling the barrier itself requires new global barrier guarantees.
assumptions_latex: \(F_i\) are valid barriers on the factors \(K_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla^2F\text{ remains block diagonal, while the KKT system may be coupled through the }A_i.

Simple-Factor Coupling Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A cross-factor perturbation that destroys convexity of a product barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the product cone \(K=\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R_+\), fix \(\varepsilon>0\) and consider \[F_\varepsilon(x_1,x_2)=-\log x_1-\log x_2+\varepsilon x_1x_2.\] Although \(F_\varepsilon\) still diverges when either coordinate approaches zero, its Hessian is \(\begin{pmatrix}x_1^{-2}&\varepsilon\\ \varepsilon&x_2^{-2}\end{pmatrix}\). At \(x_1=x_2=t\), the smallest eigenvalue equals \(t^{-2}-\varepsilon\), which is negative whenever \(t>\varepsilon^{-1/2}\). Thus even a smooth bilinear coupling of two valid simple-factor barriers can destroy convexity and therefore cannot define a self-concordant barrier on the entire product cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a positive bilinear cross-factor term to two logarithmic barriers eventually makes the Hessian indefinite, despite retaining boundary divergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(t>\varepsilon^{-1/2}\), \(\nabla^2F_\varepsilon(t,t)\) is indefinite; hence \(F_\varepsilon\) is not a barrier on all of \(K\).

Exponential-Cone Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical logarithmically homogeneous barrier for the closed exponential cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the exponential cone by \[K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:y>0,\ z>y\exp(x/y)\}.\] Its interior is equivalently described by \(y>0\), \(z>0\), and \(y\log(z/y)-x>0\). On this interior, define \[F_{\exp}(x,y,z)=-\log\!\left(y\log(z/y)-x\right)-\log y-\log z.\] This function is a \(3\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier and satisfies \(F_{\exp}(\alpha x,\alpha y,\alpha z)=F_{\exp}(x,y,z)-3\log\alpha\) for every \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential cone admits a parameter-three barrier formed from the logarithmic exponential slack together with logarithmic barriers for its positive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\exp}\) is a \(3\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier for \(K_{\exp}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy-Cone Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perspective Shannon-entropy cone and its natural logarithmic barrier candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(n\ge 1\), define the entropy cone by \[K_{\mathrm{ent}}^n=\operatorname{cl}\left\{(t,u,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R_{++}\times\mathbb R_{++}^n:t+\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log(x_i/u)\le 0\right\}.\] On its interior, with \(h(t,u,x)=-t-\sum_i x_i\log(x_i/u)>0\), the natural logarithmic barrier candidate is \[F_{\mathrm{ent}}(t,u,x)=-\log h(t,u,x)-\log u-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i.\] It diverges whenever \(h\downarrow0\), \(u\downarrow0\), or some \(x_i\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perspective entropy hypograph is a convex cone; a natural barrier logs both its entropy slack and all positive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{ent}}\) is a boundary-divergent logarithmic barrier candidate on \(\operatorname{int}K_{\mathrm{ent}}^n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cone convention and boundary-divergence claim are mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source supports the proposed entropy-cone barrier formula or its intended barrier status.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic Homogeneity of the Proposed Entropy Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic scaling claim dependent on the unaccepted entropy-barrier candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h(t,u,x)=-t-\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log(x_i/u)\) and \(F=-\log h-\log u-\sum_i\log x_i\), then formally \[F(\alpha t,\alpha u,\alpha x)=F(t,u,x)-(n+2)\log\alpha.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proposed entropy functional is formally logarithmically homogeneous of degree n+2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(\alpha t,\alpha u,\alpha x)=F(t,u,x)-(n+2)\log\alpha.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), \[K_\alpha^*=\left\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R_+^2\times\mathbb R:\left(\frac{u}{\alpha}\right)^\alpha\left(\frac{v}{1-\alpha}\right)^{1-\alpha}\ge|w|\right\}.\] The map \(T_\alpha(u,v,w)=(u/\alpha,v/(1-\alpha),w)\) sends \(K_\alpha^*\) onto \(K_\alpha\), so \(F_\alpha\circ T_\alpha\) is a parameter-three dual-cone barrier.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Power Cone and Pullback Barrier

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier status and parameter of the deferred seed's ordinary power-cone formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), \[F_\alpha(x,y,z)=-\log\!\left(x^{2\alpha}y^{2(1-\alpha)}-z^2\right)-(1-\alpha)\log x-\alpha\log y\] is a \(3\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K_\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard power-cone formula is a parameter-three self-concordant barrier for every nondegenerate exponent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\alpha\) is a \(3\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier.
knowledge_statements.title: Self-Concordance of the Power-Cone Barrier
Power-Cone Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-dimensional power cone with its standard logarithmically homogeneous barrier formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\alpha<1\), define \[K_\alpha=\left\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R:x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\ge |z|\right\}.\] On \(\operatorname{int}K_\alpha\), the standard power-cone barrier is \[F_\alpha(x,y,z)=-\log\!\left(x^{2\alpha}y^{2(1-\alpha)}-z^2\right)-(1-\alpha)\log x-\alpha\log y.\] It is logarithmically homogeneous of degree three: for every \(\tau>0\), \(F_\alpha(\tau x,\tau y,\tau z)=F_\alpha(x,y,z)-3\log\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard power-cone barrier logs the nonlinear cone slack and weighted positive coordinates, and is three-logarithmically homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\alpha(\tau x,\tau y,\tau z)=F_\alpha(x,y,z)-3\log\tau\) for every \(\tau>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The homogeneity calculation is consistent, but an authoritative source is required for the claim that the displayed expression is the standard power-cone barrier.

children.title: Generalized-Power Cone Barriers
children.top_down_role: Barrier families for multiweight power-cone extensions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Generalized-Power Cone and Pullback Barrier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation for strictly positive normalized weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha_i>0\) and \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), \[(K_\alpha^{m,q})^*=\left\{(u,w)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q:\prod_{i=1}^m\left(\frac{u_i}{\alpha_i}\right)^{\alpha_i}\ge\lVert w\rVert_2\right\}.\] Thus \(T_\alpha(u,w)=((u_i/\alpha_i)_i,w)\) maps the dual cone onto \(K_\alpha^{m,q}\), and \(F_\alpha\circ T_\alpha\) is an \((m+1)\)-parameter dual-cone barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual generalized-power cone is diagonally isomorphic to the primal cone, yielding an explicit pullback barrier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\alpha\circ T_\alpha\) is an \((m+1)\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}(K_\alpha^{m,q})^*\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Generalized-Power Cone and Pullback Barrier

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier status and parameter of the deferred seed's generalized-power formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\), \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), the function \[F_\alpha(x,z)=-\log\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^m x_i^{2\alpha_i}-\lVert z\rVert_2^2\right)-\sum_{i=1}^m(1-\alpha_i)\log x_i\] is an \((m+1)\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K_\alpha^{m,q}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The natural generalized-power formula is a self-concordant barrier with parameter m+1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\alpha\) is an \((m+1)\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier.
knowledge_statements.title: Self-Concordance of the Generalized-Power Barrier
Generalized-Power Cone Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted geometric-mean cone over a Euclidean norm and its natural homogeneous barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\) satisfy \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\). The generalized power cone is \[K_\alpha^{m,q}=\left\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R_+^m\times\mathbb R^q:\prod_{i=1}^m x_i^{\alpha_i}\ge\lVert z\rVert_2\right\}.\] On its interior, set \[F_\alpha(x,z)=-\log\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^m x_i^{2\alpha_i}-\lVert z\rVert_2^2\right)-\sum_{i=1}^m(1-\alpha_i)\log x_i.\] Then \(F_\alpha(\tau x,\tau z)=F_\alpha(x,z)-(m+1)\log\tau\) for every \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized power cone compares a weighted geometric mean with a Euclidean norm; its natural barrier is homogeneous of degree parameter m+1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\alpha(\tau x,\tau z)=F_\alpha(x,z)-(m+1)\log\tau\) for every \(\tau>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cone definition and logarithmic homogeneity are internally consistent, but the generalized barrier formula and its barrier status lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Power-Exponent Regimes
children.top_down_role: Barrier organization across admissible exponent patterns.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of exponent vectors modulo relabeling of weighted coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\), define \((\pi\alpha)_i=\alpha_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\) and \((\pi x)_i=x_{\pi^{-1}(i)}\). Then \[(x,z)\in K_\alpha^{m,q}\iff(\pi x,z)\in K_{\pi\alpha}^{m,q}.\] In particular, \((x,y,z)\mapsto(y,x,z)\) maps \(K_\alpha\) onto \(K_{1-\alpha}\), and the corresponding positive-weight barrier formulas are carried into one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permuting weighted coordinates produces an isomorphic cone and barrier; for the ordinary cone this identifies alpha with 1-alpha.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_\alpha^{m,q}\cong K_{\pi\alpha}^{m,q}\), with positive-weight barriers related by the same permutation.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponent-Permutation Isomorphisms
Power-Exponent Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible exponent domains for ordinary and generalized power cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nondegenerate three-dimensional power-cone regime is \(\alpha\in(0,1)\); both coordinate exponents are then positive and \(x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\) depends on both positive coordinates. For the generalized cone, the corresponding regime is the relative interior of the probability simplex, \[\alpha\in\Delta_m^\circ=\left\{a\in\mathbb R_{++}^m:\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=1\right\}.\] Exponents on the closed simplex boundary define valid limiting cones, but coordinates with zero exponent cease to participate in the geometric-mean inequality and must be treated as separate orthant factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nondegenerate power cones use strictly positive exponents summing to one; zero exponents produce limiting product structures with inactive coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nondegenerate regime is \(\alpha\in\Delta_m^\circ\); boundary points of \(\Delta_m\) yield factored limiting cones.

notation.meaning: Relative interior of the probability simplex

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-simplex regime is standard and the condition content kind fits the leaf, but the limiting-cone interpretation for zero exponents requires a cited convention.

children.title: Degenerate Exponent Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limiting cone behavior near exceptional exponent choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise limits of the nondegenerate barrier on the limiting cone interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[F_\alpha(x,y,z)=-\log\!\left(x^{2\alpha}y^{2(1-\alpha)}-z^2\right)-(1-\alpha)\log x-\alpha\log y,\] one has \[\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}F_\alpha(x,y,z)=-\log x-\log(y^2-z^2)\] when \(x>0\) and \(y>|z|\), and \[\lim_{\alpha\uparrow1}F_\alpha(x,y,z)=-\log(x^2-z^2)-\log y\] when \(y>0\) and \(x>|z|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At either endpoint, the power-cone barrier converges to the separable barrier for an orthant ray and a two-dimensional Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The endpoint limits are the corresponding orthant-plus-Lorentz product barriers.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Limits of Power-Cone Barriers
Degenerate Exponent Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorization of power cones when one or more exponents vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the endpoint exponents, the closed three-dimensional power cones factor as \[K_0=\mathbb R_+\times\{(y,z)\in\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R:y\ge|z|\},\qquad K_1=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R:x\ge|z|\}\times\mathbb R_+.\] More generally, if \(I_0=\{i:\alpha_i=0\}\), then \[K_\alpha^{m,q}=\mathbb R_+^{I_0}\times K_{\alpha_{I_+}}^{|I_+|,q},\qquad I_+=\{i:\alpha_i>0\}.\] Thus the strictly positive-exponent barrier formula is not directly valid at the boundary; the orthant and reduced-cone factors require separate barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an exponent reaches zero, its coordinate becomes an independent nonnegative factor, so the interior barrier must be replaced by a product barrier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_\alpha^{m,q}=\mathbb R_+^{I_0}\times K_{\alpha_{I_+}}^{|I_+|,q}\), so the positive-exponent barrier formula cannot be substituted unchanged.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated factorization follows under the convention that a zero exponent makes its coordinate inactive, but that convention and the resulting barrier limitation are uncited.

children.title: Universal Barrier Family
children.top_down_role: General barrier existence and dimension-controlled universality.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Barrier Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar-volume barrier for arbitrary proper open convex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a proper open convex set containing no affine line. For \(x\in D\), define the polar of the translated domain by \[(D-x)^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,z-x\rangle\le1\text{ for every }z\in D\}.\] Whenever this polar has finite positive volume, the universal barrier is \[U_D(x)=\log\operatorname{vol}\bigl((D-x)^\circ\bigr).\] The construction is affine invariant up to an additive constant and yields a self-concordant barrier whose parameter is bounded by a universal constant times the ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The universal barrier is the logarithm of the polar volume seen from an interior point and has dimension-controlled self-concordance.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) is proper, open, and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_D(x)=\log\operatorname{vol}((D-x)^\circ)\) is an affine-invariant, dimension-controlled self-concordant barrier.

notation.meaning: Polar of the domain translated by x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polar-volume construction is recognizable, but its precise domain hypotheses and dimension-controlled self-concordance claim require an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Volumetric Barrier Family
children.top_down_role: Volume-sensitive barriers and their geometric construction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Hessian Does Not Ensure Barrier Blow-Up
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the bare log-Hessian-volume construction without additional boundary regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(D=(-1,1)\), let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^2\). Then \(f''(x)=1>0\) throughout \(D\), but \[V_f(x)=\tfrac12\log f''(x)=0\] for every \(x\in D\). Hence \(V_f\) does not diverge as \(x\to\pm1\) and is not a barrier for \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite reference Hessian alone does not make its log determinant a barrier; a constant Hessian gives no boundary blow-up.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f''(x)>0\text{ on }D\quad\text{but}\quad V_f(x)\not\to+\infty\text{ at }\partial D.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Hessian Does Not Ensure Barrier Blow-Up

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Covariance of the Log-Hessian-Volume Functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation law under an invertible affine reparameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V_f(x)=	frac12\log\det
abla^2f(x)\). For \(B\in\operatorname{GL}(n,\mathbb R)\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(g(y)=f(By+c)\), \[
abla^2g(y)=B^T
abla^2f(By+c)B\] and \[V_g(y)=V_f(By+c)+\log|\det B|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-Hessian-volume functional is affine covariant: an invertible coordinate change adds the log absolute determinant of its linear part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V_{f\circ(By+c)}(y)=V_f(By+c)+\log|\det B|.

notation.meaning: invertible linear part of the affine coordinate change

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton evaluation architecture for a polyhedral volumetric center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At an interior iterate, form \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(b-Ax)\) and factor \(H=A^TS^{-2}A\). Reuse solves with \(H\) to compute the leverage scores and \(
abla V=A^TS^{-1}\sigma\), evaluate or assemble \(
abla^2V\) by differentiating the same weighted-Gram quantities, solve \[
abla^2V(x)\Delta x=-
abla V(x),\] and choose a line-search step preserving \(b-A(x+\alpha\Delta x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton computation reuses a weighted-Gram factorization for leverage scores, derivatives, and an interiority-preserving center step.
assumptions_latex: The Newton Hessian is nonsingular at the iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla^2V(x)\Delta x=-\nabla V(x),\qquad b-A(x+\alpha\Delta x)>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Gram Newton Computation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Leverage-Score Balance at the Volumetric Center
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order characterization for the standard polyhedral volumetric center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s=b-Ax>0\), \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), \(H=A^TS^{-2}A\), and \(V(x)=\tfrac12\log\det H\). With \[\sigma_i=(a_i/s_i)^TH^{-1}(a_i/s_i),\] one has \[\nabla V(x)=A^TS^{-1}\sigma.\] Thus an interior volumetric center satisfies \(A^TS^{-1}\sigma=0\); for the convex volumetric objective this condition is sufficient when the minimum is attained, with uniqueness under strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a volumetric center, the slack-scaled constraint normals balance when weighted by their leverage scores.
assumptions_latex: The asserted center exists in the interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla V(x)=A^TS^{-1}\sigma,\qquad \nabla V(x)=0\text{ at a volumetric center}.

notation.meaning: leverage score of scaled row i

knowledge_statements.title: Leverage-Score Balance at the Volumetric Center

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-concordance parameter and short-step consequence for a polyhedral volumetric barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the classical volumetric barrier of a full-dimensional \(n\)-dimensional polytope represented by \(m\) inequalities, its standard self-concordant-barrier parameter satisfies \[\nu_V=O(\sqrt{mn}).\] Consequently, the parameter-dependent part of a short-step path-following bound is \[O\!\left(\sqrt{\nu_V}\log(1/\varepsilon)\right)=O\!\left((mn)^{1/4}\log(1/\varepsilon)\right),\] apart from initialization and initial-gap terms. Constants depend on the self-concordance normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical polyhedral volumetric barrier has parameter order square root of mn, inducing fourth-root mn short-step dependence.
assumptions_latex: The domain is a full-dimensional polytope with \(m\) listed inequalities in \(\mathbb R^n\).
The standard volumetric-barrier and self-concordance normalizations are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu_V=O(\sqrt{mn}),\qquad N=O((mn)^{1/4}\log(1/\varepsilon)).
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Volumetric-Barrier Parameter Order
Volumetric Barrier Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-Hessian-volume construction and its standard polyhedral specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable with \(\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\) for every \(x\in D\). Define its log-Hessian-volume functional by \[V_f(x)=\frac12\log\det\nabla^2f(x).\] Additional regularity is required before this functional can be asserted to be a barrier. For a polyhedron \(D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^Tx<b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), assume that the matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), whose rows are \(a_i^T\), has full column rank. For the logarithmic barrier \(f(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(b_i-a_i^Tx)\), the standard volumetric expression is \[V_f(x)=\frac12\log\det\!\left(A^TS(x)^{-2}A\right),\qquad S(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(b-Ax).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The log-Hessian-volume functional is half the log determinant of a positive-definite reference Hessian. For a polyhedron whose constraint matrix has full column rank, the logarithmic barrier yields the standard weighted Gram-determinant formula.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\) on \(D\)
In the polyhedral specialization, \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full column rank
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_f(x)=\tfrac12\log\det\nabla^2f(x)\), and for the stated polyhedral logarithmic barrier, \(V_f(x)=\tfrac12\log\det(A^TS(x)^{-2}A)\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrix of positive polyhedral slacks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the logarithmic barrier, its Hessian, and the induced volumetric barrier on the strict feasible region of a linear-inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}\) have rows \(a_i^	op\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and let \(P^\circ=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax>b\}\). For \(x\in P^\circ\), define \(F(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(a_i^	op x-b_i)\). Its Hessian is \(
abla^2F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m rac{a_i a_i^	op}{(a_i^	op x-b_i)^2}\). Wherever \(
abla^2F(x)\succ0\), the volumetric barrier is \(v(x)= rac12\log\det(
abla^2F(x))\). Thus, up to the dimension-dependent unit-ball volume constant, \(v(x)\) is the logarithm of the inverse volume of the associated Dikin ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the strict region Ax>b, the logarithmic barrier is the negative sum of the logarithms of the slacks. Its Hessian is a sum of scaled rank-one matrices. When that Hessian is positive definite, the volumetric barrier is one half of its log determinant and equals the logarithm of the inverse Dikin-ellipsoid volume up to a dimension-dependent constant.
assumptions_latex: \nabla^2F(x)\succ0\text{ when }v(x)\text{ is interpreted as a finite real-valued log determinant}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(a_i^\top x-b_i),\qquad \nabla^2F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{a_i a_i^\top}{(a_i^\top x-b_i)^2},\qquad v(x)=\frac12\log\det(\nabla^2F(x)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Newton-decrement certificate for the volumetric barrier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local objective-gap certificate for the volumetric barrier, conditional on its minimum score parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\lambda(x)=\|\nabla v(x)\|_{Q(x)^{-1}},\qquad \varepsilon=\min_{i\in[m]}\sigma_i(x).
\]
If
\[
\lambda(x)^2\leq \frac{2\sqrt{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon}{36},
\]
then
\[
v(x)-v(x^*)\leq 2\lambda(x)^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the approximate Newton decrement is sufficiently small relative to the minimum volumetric score, twice its square bounds the volumetric-barrier objective gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v(x)-v(x^*)\leq 2\lambda(x)^2

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition induced by the Hessian determinant of an analytic barrier on a polytope with nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let E_k be a polytope with \operatorname{int}(E_k)\neq\varnothing, and let F_k be an analytic barrier for E_k. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the constraint-deletion and separating-cut branches and the computation of successive volumetric centers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a small constant \(\varepsilon\le 0.006\). Starting from a simplex \(P_0=\{x:A^{(0)}x\le b^{(0)}\}\) containing the target convex set, with \(m_0=n+1\), maintain containing polytopes \(P_t=\{x:A^{(t)}x\le b^{(t)}\}\). Let \(x_t\) minimize the volumetric barrier \(v_t\), let \(\sigma_i^{(t)}\) be the associated leverage scores at \(x_t\), and let \(F_t\) be the logarithmic barrier. If \(\min_i\sigma_i^{(t)}<\varepsilon\), delete a row attaining this minimum. Otherwise, query the separation oracle at \(x_t\) to obtain \(c^{(t)}\), choose \(\beta^{(t)}\) so that \[\frac{\bigl(\nabla^2F_t(x_t)\bigr)^{-1}[c^{(t)},c^{(t)}]}{\bigl(x_t^\top c^{(t)}-\beta^{(t)}\bigr)^2}=\frac15\sqrt{\varepsilon},\] and append the row \((c^{(t)},\beta^{(t)})\). The volumetric barrier is self-concordant and may be minimized by Newton's method; after the initial iteration, one Newton step initialized at \(x_{t-1}\) suffices for the required update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix epsilon at most 0.006 and begin with a containing simplex having n+1 inequalities. At each iteration, minimize the current polytope's volumetric barrier and compute its leverage scores. Delete an inequality if the smallest leverage score is below epsilon. Otherwise query the separation oracle at the volumetric center, shift the returned cut to satisfy the stated logarithmic-barrier Hessian normalization, and add it. The volumetric barrier is self-concordant, and the successive center update can be performed with one Newton step initialized at the preceding center.
assumptions_latex: P_0\text{ is a simplex containing the target convex set and }m_0=n+1
P_t=\{x:A^{(t)}x\le b^{(t)}\}\text{ contains the target convex set}
\sigma_i^{(t)}\text{ are the leverage scores of }v_t\text{ at }x_t
c^{(t)}\text{ is supplied by a separation-oracle query at }x_t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{t+1}\text{ is obtained either by deleting an inequality attaining }\min_i\sigma_i^{(t)}<\varepsilon\text{, or by adding the normalized separating inequality }(c^{(t)})^\top x\le\beta^{(t)};\text{ the volumetric-center update is Newton-computable, with one warm-started step sufficient after initialization.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path-Following Complexity for a Strictly Feasible Standard-Form Linear Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The displayed minimum presupposes a finite attained optimal value. The extract identifies only a standard path-following method based on approximate Newton steps and does not specify its initialization or neighborhood policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}^m$, $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and $F(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\ln x^{(i)}$. Suppose $\mathcal F^\circ=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbb{R}^n_+)\}\neq\varnothing$, the restriction $F_{\mid}$ is an $n$-self-concordant barrier on $\mathcal F^\circ$, and the displayed primal minimum $p^\star=\min\{\langle c,u\rangle:Au=b,\ u\in\mathbb{R}^n_+\}$ is finite and attained. For an accuracy $0<\epsilon<n$, a standard central-path-following method based on approximate Newton steps produces $x$ satisfying $$\langle c,x\rangle-p^\star\le\epsilon$$ in $$O\!\left(\sqrt n\,\ln\frac{n}{\epsilon}\right)$$ Newton iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a standard-form linear program with a strictly feasible point and a finite attained optimum, assume that the standard logarithmic barrier restricted to the strictly feasible affine set is an n-self-concordant barrier. In the nontrivial accuracy regime, the stated standard central-path method obtains objective gap at most epsilon in O(sqrt(n) log(n/epsilon)) Newton iterations.
assumptions_latex: F_{\mid}\text{ is an }n\text{-self-concordant barrier on }\mathcal F^\circ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle c,x\rangle-p^\star\le\epsilon\quad\text{after}\quad O\!\left(\sqrt n\ln\frac n\epsilon\right)\text{ Newton iterations}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier Function and Primal Central Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a barrier, its extended-value convention, the associated primal central path, and the path-following update principle. The extract's convergence assertion is not retained because boundary divergence and strict convexity alone do not provide all required existence, optimal-solution, and limit hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) have nonempty interior. A function \(F:\operatorname{int}(\mathcal X)\to\mathbb R\) is a barrier for \(\mathcal X\) if \(F(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\to\partial\mathcal X\). For a strictly convex barrier, extend \(F\) by \(F(x)=+\infty\) outside \(\operatorname{int}(\mathcal X)\). For each considered \(t\in\mathbb R_+\) for which a minimizer exists, set \(F_t(x)=t c^\top x+F(x)\) and choose \(x^*(t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}F_t(x)\). The family \((x^*(t))_t\) is the primal central path. A barrier path-following step uses \(x^*(t)\) to initialize a fast local method for \(F_{t'}\), where \(t'>t\) is chosen to balance path progress with retention of local fast convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A barrier tends to positive infinity at the feasible-set boundary and is assigned positive infinity outside the interior. Minimizers of the scaled linear objective plus a strictly convex barrier form the primal central path whenever those minimizers exist. Path following increases the scale while using the previous path point to initialize a local solver.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is strictly convex for the central-path construction}
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{t c^\top x+F(x)\}\neq\varnothing\quad\text{for every considered }t\in\mathbb R_+
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^*(t))_t\text{ is the primal central path, and a path-following update proceeds from }t\text{ to some }t'>t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A barrier-based three-stage process with a separate boundary case when the initial truncation parameter is nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose $z_0\in\operatorname{int}S$ and $\Delta>0$, and set $\alpha=\langle d,z_0\rangle+\Delta$. If $\alpha\leq0$, use the stated two-stage process. If $\alpha>0$, perform three stages:

1. On $S(\alpha)$ use
\[
\widetilde F(z)=F(z)-\ln\bigl(\alpha-\langle d,z\rangle\bigr)
\]
to find $\widetilde z$ satisfying $\lambda_{\widetilde F}(\widetilde z)\leq\beta$.

2. Follow the central path
\[
td+\widetilde F'(z(t))=0,\qquad t\geq0,
\]
toward the minimizer of $\langle d,z\rangle$ over $S(\alpha)$. Under the Slater condition its optimal value is negative. Define
\[
\bar S=\{z\in S(\alpha):\langle d,z\rangle\leq0\},\qquad
\bar F(z)=\widetilde F(z)-\ln\bigl(-\langle d,z\rangle\bigr).
\]
The analytic center $z_*$ of $\bar S$ satisfies
\[
\widetilde F'(z_*)-\frac{d}{\langle d,z_*\rangle}=0,
\qquad t_*=-\frac1{\langle d,z_*\rangle}>0.
\]
Continue until a point $\bar z$ satisfies the stated $\beta$-neighborhood condition for this center equation.

3. The asserted Hessian comparison transfers this neighborhood guarantee to $\bar F$, so apply the main path-following scheme to
\[
\min\{\langle c,z\rangle:z\in\bar S\},
\]
which is equivalent to problem (4.2.31).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from an interior point and a positive initial gap. If the resulting truncation level is nonpositive, use the earlier two-stage method. Otherwise, first approximate the analytic center of a truncated feasible section, then follow an auxiliary central path until reaching a neighborhood of the analytic center of the additionally truncated set where the d-objective is nonpositive, and finally run the main path-following scheme for the original objective. Under Slater's condition, the intermediate optimum is strictly negative and the final restricted problem is equivalent to the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{\langle c,z\rangle:z\in\bar S\}\ \text{is equivalent to problem (4.2.31), and the main path-following scheme can be initialized from }\bar z

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-Determinant Analytic Center of a Strict LMI
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the log-determinant barrier and analytic center of a nonempty bounded strict LMI region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F(x)=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iF_i with F_i=F_i^T, and set \phi(x)=\log\det(F(x)^{-1}) when F(x)\succ0 and \phi(x)=+\infty otherwise. The function \phi is finite exactly on \{x:F(x)\succ0\} and tends to +\infty as x approaches its boundary. If this feasible set is nonempty and bounded, then \phi is strictly convex on it and has a unique minimizer x^\star, called the analytic center. Equivalently, x^\star=\arg\max_{F(x)\succ0}\det F(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative log-determinant is a barrier for a strict affine LMI region. If that region is nonempty and bounded, it has a unique analytic center, equivalently the feasible point whose matrix has maximum determinant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star=\arg\min_x\phi(x)=\arg\max_{F(x)\succ0}\det F(x)\text{ exists uniquely}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path of Centers for an Eigenvalue/LMI Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the analytic-center path of bounded strict objective-level sections and records its stationarity, analyticity, and limiting behavior without asserting strict feasibility of the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F(x)=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iF_i with F_i=F_i^T, and let \lambda^{\mathrm{opt}}=\inf\{c^Tx:F(x)\succ0\}. Suppose that for each \lambda>\lambda^{\mathrm{opt}}, the set \{x:F(x)\succ0,\ c^Tx<\lambda\} is nonempty and bounded. Define x^\star(\lambda)=\arg\min_x\left(\log\det(F(x)^{-1})+\log\frac{1}{\lambda-c^Tx}\right). The curve x^\star(\lambda), \lambda>\lambda^{\mathrm{opt}}, is the path of centers. It is analytic and has a limit x^{\mathrm{opt}} as \lambda\downarrow\lambda^{\mathrm{opt}}; the points x^\star(\lambda) form a feasible minimizing sequence, although the limit need not remain strictly feasible. They satisfy -\operatorname{Tr}(F(x^\star(\lambda))^{-1}F_i)+\frac{c_i}{\lambda-c^Tx^\star(\lambda)}=0 for i=1,\ldots,m.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every objective level above the infimum, take the analytic center of the bounded section cut out by the strict LMI and objective bound. These centers form an analytic path and a feasible minimizing sequence with a limit as the level decreases to the optimum; the limit is not asserted to remain strictly feasible. Each center satisfies the stated barrier stationarity equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^\star(\lambda)=\arg\min_x\left(\log\det(F(x)^{-1})+\log\frac{1}{\lambda-c^Tx}\right),\quad \lim_{\lambda\downarrow\lambda^{\mathrm{opt}}}x^\star(\lambda)=x^{\mathrm{opt}},\quad c^Tx^\star(\lambda)\to\lambda^{\mathrm{opt}}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be bounded with nonempty interior. For x\in C, define \operatorname{depth}(x,C)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C). A Chebyshev center is any x_{\mathrm{cheb}}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in C}\operatorname{depth}(x,C), whenever this argmax is nonempty. The depth is the radius of the largest ball centered at x and contained in C, so a Chebyshev center is the center of a largest ball contained in C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded set with nonempty interior, the depth of a point is its distance from the complement. Any point attaining maximum depth is a Chebyshev center; equivalently, it centers a largest ball contained in the set.

knowledge_statements.title: Analytic Center Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness for a bounded affine feasible region with a strictly convex barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a nonempty bounded open convex subset of an affine space \(L\subset\mathbb R^n\). Suppose \(F:Q\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and strictly convex, and \(F(x_k)\to+\infty\) for every sequence \((x_k)\subset Q\) converging to the relative boundary of \(Q\). Then there exists a unique point \(x_c\in Q\) satisfying \[F(x_c)=\min_{x\in Q}F(x).\] This minimizer is the analytic center of \(Q\) relative to the barrier \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous strictly convex barrier that diverges at the boundary of a bounded feasible region has a unique analytic center.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is nonempty, bounded, open, and convex relative to an affine space
\(F\) is continuous and strictly convex on \(Q\)
\(F\) diverges along every approach to the relative boundary
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}F(x)=\{x_c\}\) for a unique \(x_c\in Q\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence on a possibly unbounded feasible section through one compact barrier sublevel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional affine space and let \(F:Q\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and strictly convex. If for some \(x_0\in Q\) the sublevel \[L_0=\{x\in Q:F(x)\leq F(x_0)\}\] is compact relative to \(\operatorname{aff}Q\), then \(F\) attains its minimum on \(Q\), and the minimizer is unique. Thus boundedness of \(Q\) is sufficient but not necessary for analytic-center existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One nonempty compact barrier sublevel guarantees attainment, and strict convexity guarantees uniqueness, even if the feasible section is unbounded.

\(F:Q\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and strictly convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Analytic Center Location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order characterization of an analytic center on an affine slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=\{x\in D:Ax=b\}\), where \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open and convex, \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), and \(F:D\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and strictly convex on \(Q\). A point \(x_c\in Q\) is the analytic center exactly when there exists \(y_c\in\mathbb R^p\) such that \[\nabla F(x_c)+A^Ty_c=0.\] Equivalently, \(\langle\nabla F(x_c),d\rangle=0\) for every feasible direction \(d\in\ker A\). Under existence, strict convexity makes this location unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The analytic center is the feasible point whose barrier gradient is orthogonal to every affine feasible direction; strict convexity makes it unique.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is differentiable and strictly convex on \(Q\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_c\) is the analytic center if and only if \(Ax_c=b\) and there exists \(y_c\in\mathbb R^p\) such that \(\nabla F(x_c)+A^Ty_c=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Centering Level-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative compactness of barrier sublevel sets on an affine feasible slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and define \(Q=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\). Let \(F:Q\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and suppose \(F(x_k)\to+\infty\) whenever a sequence \((x_k)\subset Q\) approaches the relative boundary of \(Q\) in \(H=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}\). For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), define \(L_\alpha=\{x\in Q:F(x)\leq\alpha\}\). If \(L_\alpha\) is bounded, then it is compact relative to \(H\). Thus every nonempty bounded barrier sublevel is separated from the relative boundary of the feasible slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary blow-up makes each bounded barrier sublevel closed in the affine feasible slice and therefore relatively compact.

\(F\) diverges along sequences approaching the relative boundary of \(Q\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dikin Geometry of Centered Level Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative local shape of self-concordant barrier level sets around a stationary analytic center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a standard self-concordant barrier and let \(x_c\) minimize \(F\) on an affine feasible slice. For a feasible displacement \(h\), set \(r=\|h\|_{x_c}=\sqrt{h^T\nabla^2F(x_c)h}\). If \(r<1\), then \(x_c+h\) remains in the barrier domain and \[\omega(r)\leq F(x_c+h)-F(x_c)\leq\omega_*(r),\qquad \omega(r)=r-\log(1+r),\quad \omega_*(r)=-r-\log(1-r).\] Consequently, the unit Dikin ball in the affine slice lies in the domain, and these inequalities give local inner and outer local-norm bounds for centered sublevels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Self-concordance bounds centered barrier sublevels by local-norm balls and places the unit Dikin ball inside the feasible domain.
assumptions_latex: \(x_c\) minimizes \(F\) on the affine feasible slice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_c+h\) is in the barrier domain and \(\omega(r)\leq F(x_c+h)-F(x_c)\leq\omega_*(r)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Centering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Examples showing how loss of level-boundedness or strict convexity can destroy analytic-center existence or uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Existence and uniqueness can fail through different mechanisms. On \(Q_1=(0,\infty)\), the barrier \(F(x)=-\log x\) satisfies \(\inf_{x\in Q_1}F(x)=-\infty\), so it has no minimizer. For a loss-of-uniqueness example, define \(Q_2=(0,1)^2\), \(f(u)=-\log u-\log(1-u)\), and
\[
h(v)=\begin{cases}-\log(3v),&0<v<1/3,\\0,&1/3\leq v\leq2/3,\\-\log(3(1-v)),&2/3<v<1.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(G(u,v)=f(u)+h(v)\) is convex and diverges at the boundary of \(Q_2\), but its minimizer set is \(\{1/2\}\times[1/3,2/3]\). Thus unbounded sublevels can cause nonattainment, while failure of strict convexity along feasible directions can permit nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbounded barrier sublevels can prevent attainment, and flat feasible directions can produce multiple analytic centers even when the centering function diverges at the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Loss of level-boundedness can cause nonexistence, and loss of strict convexity can permit nonuniqueness.

notation.meaning: open convex feasible regions in the two examples
centering functions in the two examples

The condition \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}Q=\varnothing\) does not by itself imply failure of analytic centering. If \(F\) is a continuous barrier on \(\operatorname{ri}_H Q\), is strictly convex along \(H-H\), and has a nonempty compact sublevel relative to \(H\), then \(F\) has a unique relative analytic center. Failure occurs if an ambient-interior barrier is incorrectly required or if the corresponding relative attainment or curvature hypotheses fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional feasible section can have a unique relative analytic center; empty ambient interior is a formulation boundary, not automatic nonexistence.

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier Homotopy Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal barrier family for a finite-dimensional conic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic program \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), let \(F\) be a barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\) and define \(Q=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:Ax=b\}\). The objective-weight barrier homotopy is the indexed family
\[
\min_{x\in Q}\Phi_t(x),\qquad \Phi_t(x)=t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x),\qquad t>0.
\]
Whenever the problem at each \(t>0\) has a unique minimizer, denote it by \(x(t)\). The set \(\{x(t):t>0\}\) is the primal barrier path associated with this homotopy convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The barrier homotopy is the family obtained by adding a barrier to a positively weighted conic objective; when its minimizers are unique, they form the primal barrier path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever it exists uniquely, \(x(t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}\{t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x)\}\) for each \(t>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Path Parameter Choices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent objective-weight, barrier-weight, and logarithmic parameter conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define \(\mu=t^{-1}\) and \(\theta=\log t\). Multiplication of an objective by a positive scalar does not change its minimizers, so
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}\{t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x)\}
=
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}\{\langle c,x\rangle+\mu F(x)\}.
\]
Thus \(t\uparrow\infty\) is the same endpoint regime as \(\mu\downarrow0\), while \(\theta\in\mathbb R\) provides an unconstrained parameter. The convention must be stated because increasing \(t\) and increasing \(\mu\) move in opposite directions along the same path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective weight, barrier weight, and log weight describe the same path via reciprocal or logarithmic changes of parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(t\)- and \(\mu\)-parameterized problems have identical minimizer sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Reparameterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of the geometric central path under monotone parameter changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I,J\subseteq\mathbb R\) be intervals, let \(x:I\to Q\) parameterize a barrier path, and let \(\varphi:J\to I\) be a continuous strictly monotone bijection. Then \(\widetilde x=x\circ\varphi\) has exactly the same image:
\[
\{\widetilde x(\tau):\tau\in J\}=\{x(t):t\in I\}.
\]
If \(x\) and \(\varphi\) are differentiable, then \(\widetilde x'(\tau)=x'(\varphi(\tau))\varphi'(\tau)\). Hence reparameterization preserves path points and their order up to orientation, but changes speed and reverses orientation when \(\varphi\) is decreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous monotone bijection changes only the path’s parameter, speed, and possibly orientation, not its geometric image.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi:J\to I\) is a continuous strictly monotone bijection
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{im}(x\circ\varphi)=\operatorname{im}(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Homotopy Endpoint Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Centering and optimization endpoint limits of a finite-dimensional primal barrier family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, let \(Q=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\), and let \(F:Q\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Suppose \(x(t)\) uniquely minimizes \(t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x)\) over \(Q\) for every \(t>0\). If \(F\) has a unique minimizer \(x_{\mathrm{ac}}\) and there are \(t_0>0\) and a compact set \(C\subset Q\) with \(x(t)\in C\) for \(0<t\leq t_0\), then \(x(t)\to x_{\mathrm{ac}}\) as \(t\downarrow0\). If the conic problem has nonempty optimal set \(X^*\) and \(\{x(t):t\geq t_1\}\) is bounded for some \(t_1>0\), then every accumulation point as \(t\uparrow\infty\) belongs to \(X^*\). If those accumulation points consist of a single point, the entire large-parameter path converges to that point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact containment near zero forces convergence to the analytic center, while bounded large-parameter path points can accumulate only at conic optima.
assumptions_latex: Each barrier problem has a unique minimizer \(x(t)\)
The small-parameter path is contained in a compact subset of \(Q\)
For the large-parameter claim, \(X^*\neq\varnothing\) and the path tail is bounded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(t)\to x_{\mathrm{ac}}\) as \(t\downarrow0\), and every large-parameter accumulation point lies in \(X^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Central-Path Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of every primal path point under compact-sublevel and strict-convexity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and define \(Q=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\). Let \(F:Q\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and strictly convex along every nonzero feasible direction. For \(t>0\), define \(\Phi_t(x)=t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x)\). If every nonempty sublevel set \(\{x\in Q:\Phi_t(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact relative to \(\{x:Ax=b\}\), then \(\Phi_t\) attains its minimum at a unique point \(x(t)\in Q\). If this condition holds for every \(t>0\), the primal central path \(t\mapsto x(t)\) exists throughout the positive parameter range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness of every nonempty penalized sublevel gives attainment, and strict convexity gives a unique primal central-path point at every positive parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuous and strictly convex on feasible directions
For every \(t>0\), every nonempty sublevel of \(\Phi_t\) is relatively compact
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t>0\), there exists a unique \(x(t)\in Q\) minimizing \(t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Path Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of primal-dual path triples induced by an attained differentiable primal barrier family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), let \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and define \(Q=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\). Let \(F:Q\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and strictly convex on feasible directions, and suppose \(-\nabla F(x)\in\operatorname{int}K^*\) for every \(x\in Q\). Assume that for each \(\mu>0\), the problem \(\min_{x\in Q}\{\langle c,x\rangle+\mu F(x)\}\) has a minimizer \(x(\mu)\). Then there exists \(y(\mu)\in\mathbb R^m\) such that, with \(s(\mu)=-\mu\nabla F(x(\mu))\),
\[
Ax(\mu)=b,\qquad A^*y(\mu)+s(\mu)=c,\qquad s(\mu)\in\operatorname{int}K^*.
\]
Thus a strictly feasible primal-dual path triple exists for every \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each attained differentiable barrier problem yields an equality multiplier and an interior dual slack, producing a primal-dual path triple.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is differentiable and strictly convex on feasible directions
Each primal barrier problem is attained
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\mu>0\), there exists \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) satisfying primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and \(s(\mu)=-\mu\nabla F(x(\mu))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\), let \(F\) be differentiable and convex on \(Q\), and fix \(\mu>0\). For \(x\in Q\),
\[
x\in\arg\min_{z\in Q}\{\langle c,z\rangle+\mu F(z)\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ c+\mu\nabla F(x)=A^*y.
\]
Equivalently, setting \(s=-\mu\nabla F(x)\) gives \(Ax=b\) and \(A^*y+s=c\). If \(-\nabla F(x)\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), then \(s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\). Strict convexity on feasible directions ensures uniqueness of \(x\) but is unnecessary for the equivalence.

children.title: Central-Path Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions governing a single central trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Path Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of primal-dual path triples under strict convexity and independent equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) have full row rank, and define \(Q=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:Ax=b\}\). Fix \(\mu>0\). Suppose \(F:Q\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and strictly convex along every nonzero direction in \(\ker A\), and suppose \(\langle c,x\rangle+\mu F(x)\) attains its minimum on \(Q\). Then its minimizer \(x(\mu)\) is unique. The relation \(s(\mu)=-\mu\nabla F(x(\mu))\) uniquely fixes the slack, and injectivity of \(A^*\) uniquely fixes any multiplier satisfying \(A^*y(\mu)+s(\mu)=c\). Consequently, if a primal-dual central-path triple exists at \(\mu\), it is unique; under the primal-dual existence conditions, exactly one such triple exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity fixes the primal point and slack, while full row rank fixes the multiplier, so an existing primal-dual path triple is unique.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is differentiable and strictly convex on nonzero directions in \(\ker A\)
The barrier problem at \(\mu>0\) is attained
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most one triple \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) satisfies the central-path relations; with existence, exactly one does.

source_refs.locator: 5.5 Existence of the central path - a constructive proof p. 124

source_witnesses.locator: 5.5 Existence of the central path - a constructive proof p. 124

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Redundant Equalities Can Destroy Multiplier Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness of full row rank for uniqueness of the entire primal-dual path triple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\mathbb R_+\), let \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be the zero map, and take \(b=0\), \(c=1\), and \(F(x)=-\log x\). For every \(\mu>0\), the barrier objective \(x-\mu\log x\) has the unique minimizer \(x(\mu)=\mu\), and \(s(\mu)=-\mu F'(x(\mu))=1\). Nevertheless,
\[A^*y+s=c\]
holds for every \(y\in\mathbb R\). Thus the primal point and slack are unique while the multiplier, and hence the full path triple, is not unique when the equality map lacks full row rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A redundant equality coordinate can leave the primal point and slack unique while making the equality multiplier arbitrary.
assumptions_latex: \(A=0\), so the equality map lacks full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(\mu)=\mu\) and \(s(\mu)=1\) are unique, but every \(y\in\mathbb R\) satisfies the multiplier equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Equalities Can Destroy Multiplier Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.title: Embedded Path Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence criterion for a homogeneous self-dual embedding path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a homogeneous self-dual embedding have affine equations \(\mathcal A z=d\), cone \(\mathcal K\), and a differentiable strictly convex barrier \(\mathcal F\) on \(\operatorname{int}\mathcal K\). Assume there exists \(z^0\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal K\) satisfying \(\mathcal A z^0=d\), and that for every \(\mu>0\) the embedded barrier objective \(z\mapsto\langle q,z\rangle+\mu\mathcal F(z)\) has compact sublevel sets on the embedded affine slice. Then it has a unique minimizer \(z(\mu)\) for every \(\mu>0\); hence the embedded central path exists throughout the positive parameter range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly feasible embedding with strictly convex, level-bounded barrier objectives has a unique embedded path point for every positive parameter.
assumptions_latex: The embedded affine slice meets \(\operatorname{int}\mathcal K\)
\(\mathcal F\) is differentiable and strictly convex on embedded feasible directions
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\mu>0\), the embedded barrier problem has a unique solution \(z(\mu)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied, and the affine objective formulation is not tied to a specific homogeneous self-dual embedding convention. An authoritative source with an embedding definition and path-existence locator is required before the mathematical scope can be assessed reliably.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines centrality for a feasible positive-definite embedded primal-dual pair at fixed barrier parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mu\in(0,1)\) and a feasible positive-definite pair \((\widetilde X,\widetilde S)\), let \(V^2=\widetilde X^{1/2}\widetilde S\widetilde X^{1/2}\). Define
\[
\delta(\widetilde X,\widetilde S,\mu):=\frac{1}{2\sqrt\mu}\lVert D_V\rVert=\frac12\left\lVert \sqrt\mu V^{-1}-\frac1{\sqrt\mu}V\right\rVert.
\]
Then \(\delta(\widetilde X,\widetilde S,\mu)\ge 0\), with equality if and only if \(\widetilde X\widetilde S=\mu I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible positive-definite embedded primal-dual pair and a fixed parameter between zero and one, the NT centrality distance is half the norm of the scaled difference between the inverse and direct scaling matrices. It is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at complementarity X S = μI.
assumptions_latex: (\widetilde X,\widetilde S)\text{ is feasible and positive definite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(\widetilde X,\widetilde S,\mu)\ge 0,\qquad \delta(\widetilde X,\widetilde S,\mu)=0\iff \widetilde X\widetilde S=\mu I.

children.title: Path Existence Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degenerate or non-strictly feasible settings obstructing standard path guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Existence Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mechanisms that can prevent existence or single-valuedness of an interior central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A central path can fail to exist throughout the positive parameter range when strict feasibility or attainment fails, and it can fail to be single-valued when strict convexity is absent. For example, the conic problem \(\min\{-x:x\geq0\}\) with barrier \(F(x)=-\log x\) has penalized objective \(-tx-\log x\), which is unbounded below for every \(t>0\); hence it has no path point. If \(Q=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing\), no primal interior path is possible. If a barrier objective is attained but has multiple minimizers because it is flat along feasible directions, the associated path correspondence is set-valued rather than a single curve. These are failure mechanisms, not necessary consequences of every loss of strict convexity or level-boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empty strict feasibility or nonattainment can eliminate path points, while flat feasible directions can make the path set-valued; these failures are possible rather than automatic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility alone does not guarantee a path point, and loss of strict convexity can permit a non-single-valued path.

source_refs.locator: 5.5 Existence of the central path - a constructive proof p. 124

source_witnesses.locator: 5.5 Existence of the central path - a constructive proof p. 124

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary dual-interiority condition for a strictly interior coupled central path; it is not sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If a primal-dual path point satisfies \(A^*y(\mu)+s(\mu)=c\) with \(s(\mu)\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), then \(c-A^*y(\mu)\in\operatorname{int}K^*\). Consequently,
\[
\{y\in\mathbb R^m:c-A^*y\in\operatorname{int}K^*\}=\varnothing
\]
precludes every strictly interior primal-dual path point. Nonemptiness of this set is not sufficient: primal strict feasibility and attainment may still fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the dual-slack affine space misses the interior of the dual cone, no strictly interior primal-dual central-path point exists.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone with nonempty interior.
A strictly interior path point must satisfy \(A^*y+s=c\) and \(s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{y:c-A^*y\in\operatorname{int}K^*\}=\varnothing\Rightarrow\) no strictly interior primal-dual path point exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Interiority Obstruction

children.title: Complementarity Product Geometry
children.top_down_role: Cone-dependent geometry of primal-dual complementarity products.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Product Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite primal-dual complementarity represented by a symmetric positive-definite product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X,S\in\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\), define \(W=X^{1/2}SX^{1/2}\) and \(\mu=\langle X,S\rangle/n\). Then \(W\in\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\), \(W\) is similar to \(XS\), and
\[\operatorname{tr}W=\langle X,S\rangle=n\mu.\]
Moreover, \(XS=\mu I\) holds if and only if \(W=\mu I\). Thus departure of the complementarity product from the central ray is represented without ambiguity by the symmetric residual \(W-\mu I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric product X^(1/2)SX^(1/2) has the spectrum and trace of complementarity, and it equals μI exactly at primal-dual centrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\succ0\), \(\operatorname{tr}W=n\mu\), and \(XS=\mu I\iff W=\mu I\).

children.title: Spectral Complementarity Measures
children.top_down_role: Eigenvalue-based descriptions of complementarity imbalance.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_{\infty}(X,S)=0\iff X^{1/2}SX^{1/2}=\mu I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eigenvalue-based measures of semidefinite complementarity centrality.

source_refs.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X,S\in\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\), let \(W=X^{1/2}SX^{1/2}\), \(\mu=\operatorname{tr}(W)/n\), and let \(\lambda_i(W)\) denote the eigenvalues of \(W\). The relative spectral deviations are
\[\delta_i=\frac{\lambda_i(W)}{\mu}-1.\]
The spectral centrality radius and lower centrality ratio are, respectively,
\[\delta_{\infty}(X,S)=\max_i|\delta_i|,\qquad \rho_{-}(X,S)=\frac{\lambda_{\min}(W)}{\mu}.\]
Exact complementarity centrality is equivalent to \(\delta_{\infty}(X,S)=0\), or equivalently \(\rho_{-}(X,S)=1\) together with \(\operatorname{tr}(W)=n\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized eigenvalue deviations measure how far the symmetric complementarity product is from the scalar matrix μI; they vanish exactly at complementarity centrality.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Complementarity Measures

source_witnesses.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral Radius Bounds and Positivity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided spectral control and its sharp radius-only positivity boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(W=X^{1/2}SX^{1/2}\succ0\), \(\mu=\operatorname{tr}(W)/n\), \(\delta_i=\lambda_i(W)/\mu-1\), and \(\delta_\infty=\max_i|\delta_i|\). Then
\[
(1-\delta_\infty)\mu\leq\lambda_i(W)\leq(1+\delta_\infty)\mu,
\qquad
\rho_-:=\frac{\lambda_{\min}(W)}{\mu}=1+\min_i\delta_i\geq1-\delta_\infty.
\]
If \(\delta_\infty<1\), then
\[
\kappa_2(W)\leq\frac{1+\delta_\infty}{1-\delta_\infty}.
\]
For \(n\geq2\), the threshold is sharp for a radius-only lower bound: normalized positive spectra of mean one can satisfy \(\delta_\infty\uparrow1\) while their minimum component tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spectral radius confines every complementarity eigenvalue to (1±δ)μ; below one it bounds conditioning, and one is the sharp radius-only positivity threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-\delta_\infty)\mu\leq\lambda_i(W)\leq(1+\delta_\infty)\mu\), and \(\delta_\infty<1\Rightarrow\kappa_2(W)\leq(1+\delta_\infty)/(1-\delta_\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Radius Bounds and Positivity Boundary

children.title: Centrality Residual Geometry
children.top_down_role: Residual organizations measuring displacement from centrality.

knowledge_statements.title: Centrality Residual Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm geometry of the symmetric semidefinite centrality residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X,S\in\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\), set \(W=X^{1/2}SX^{1/2}\), \(\mu=\operatorname{tr}(W)/n\), and \(R=W-\mu I\). Then \(R\in\mathbb S^{n}\), \(\operatorname{tr}R=0\), and
\[\|R\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(\lambda_i(W)-\mu\bigr)^2.\]
Consequently, \(\|R\|_{2}\leq\|R\|_{F}\leq\sqrt n\,\|R\|_{2}\), and \(R=0\) if and only if every complementarity eigenvalue equals \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The centrality residual is trace-free, and its Frobenius norm is exactly the Euclidean dispersion of complementarity eigenvalues around μ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{tr}R=0\) and \(\|R\|_F^2=\sum_i(\lambda_i(W)-\mu)^2\).
