children.title: Ill-Posed Status Boundary
children.top_down_role: Outcomes for which finite-precision evidence does not robustly distinguish nearby statuses.

children.title: Ill-Posed Conic Instances
children.top_down_role: Instances lying near boundaries between conic status classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional conic family exhibiting zero status-stability radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+\), consider \(x=t\), \(x\in K\). The system is feasible for \(t\ge0\) and infeasible for \(t<0\). Hence \(t=0\) lies on the feasibility-status boundary: every neighborhood contains both feasible and infeasible data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalar nonnegative feasibility system changes status at zero under arbitrarily small right-hand-side perturbations.
assumptions_latex: The scalar datum \(t\) is measured in the absolute-value norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance \(t=0\) has zero feasibility-status stability radius.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Feasibility Boundary Instance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Status-Preserving Radius for a Declared Feasibility Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric stability after fixing a feasibility-status partition, admissible perturbations, and data norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) and \(\mathcal I\) be complementary feasible- and infeasible-data sets in a finite-dimensional normed data space, and suppose their common boundary is \(\Sigma=\partial\mathcal F=\partial\mathcal I\). For \(D\notin\Sigma\), \[\rho(D)=\operatorname{dist}(D,\Sigma)\] is the supremum of radii \(r\) for which the open ball \(B(D,r)\) remains in the same status set as \(D\). Thus positive radius gives local status stability, while boundary data have radius zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed feasibility partition, distance to its boundary is the largest open perturbation radius guaranteed to preserve status.
assumptions_latex: The data space, norm, admissible perturbations, and feasible/infeasible partition are fixed.
The two status sets have the declared common boundary \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(D)=\operatorname{dist}(D,\Sigma)\) is the maximal open status-preserving radius.
review_flags: This conditional metric fact does not select among primal, dual, solvability, or homogeneous combined ill-posed sets.
The radius is absolute rather than scale invariant.
knowledge_statements.title: Status-Preserving Radius for a Declared Feasibility Partition

assumptions_latex: Conic problem data \(D=(A,b,c)\) lie in a finite-dimensional normed data space.
Let \(\mathcal F\) and \(\mathcal I\) denote data sets having, respectively, feasible and infeasible primal constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance is ill-posed precisely when \(D\in\overline{\mathcal F}\cap\overline{\mathcal I}\), equivalently when its distance to the primal feasibility-status boundary is zero.

notation.meaning: Sets of primal-feasible and primal-infeasible data.
Closure in the selected data norm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-feasibility ill-posedness in a fixed finite-dimensional normed data model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conic instance with data \(D=(A,b,c)\) is ill-posed for primal feasibility when \[D\in\overline{\mathcal F}\cap\overline{\mathcal I}.\] Thus every neighborhood of \(D\) contains data with a feasible primal system and data with an infeasible primal system. Equivalently, if \(\Sigma=\overline{\mathcal F}\cap\overline{\mathcal I}\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(D,\Sigma)=0\). Dual or combined ill-posedness is defined analogously using the corresponding status sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance is ill-posed when arbitrarily small data perturbations can switch its feasibility status, placing it on the closure boundary between feasible and infeasible data.
knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Posed Conic Instances

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary definition is plausible for primal-feasibility ill-posedness, but no source establishes the chosen status sets, topology, data model, or the convention being called ill-posed.

children.title: Indeterminate Solver Status
children.top_down_role: Outcomes lacking reliable classification from available numerical evidence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent minimal interpretation of an indeterminate classification under declared validators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a solver interface with declared acceptance predicates \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) for all solution and status-certificate outcomes it can validate. If a completed classification attempt satisfies \(\neg P_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\neg P_m\), its classification outcome is indeterminate. This states only that the available run validated none of the declared conclusions; it neither assigns an exact mathematical status to the conic instance nor shows that no valid certificate exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every declared status validator fails, the run is classification-indeterminate, which is absence of validated evidence rather than an exact problem status.
assumptions_latex: The interface's supported status predicates and their tolerances are declared.
The outcome concerns a completed classification attempt, not an interruption or unsupported input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of every declared predicate warrants only an indeterminate classification outcome.

notation.meaning: Declared solution and certificate acceptance predicates.

review_flags: Iteration limits, user interruption, unsupported structure, and internal numerical failure should remain distinct operational statuses when the interface distinguishes them.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Inconclusive Solver Outcome

assumptions_latex: A solver uses stated tolerances to test approximate optimality, infeasibility, and unboundedness certificates.
At termination, none of the accepted status predicates is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mathematically warranted solver status is indeterminate; no exact feasibility or infeasibility conclusion follows from termination alone.

notation.meaning: Primal and dual residual acceptance tolerances.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: solver status is defined by failure of all declared acceptance predicates
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational status when a finite-precision run validates neither a solution nor a status certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_{\mathrm{opt}}\), \(P_{\mathrm{pinf}}\), \(P_{\mathrm{dinf}}\), \(P_{\mathrm{punb}}\), and \(P_{\mathrm{dunb}}\) be the solver's declared acceptance predicates. The returned status is indeterminate when \[
eg P_{\mathrm{opt}}\wedge
eg P_{\mathrm{pinf}}\wedge
eg P_{\mathrm{dinf}}\wedge
eg P_{\mathrm{punb}}\wedge
eg P_{\mathrm{dunb}}.\] This status records absence of a validated conclusion; it is not itself a certificate that the original conic problem has any particular exact status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run is indeterminate when no declared solution or certificate test passes; this absence of validation implies no exact problem status.
knowledge_statements.title: Indeterminate Solver Status

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is a reasonable operational definition, but the collection of acceptance predicates and the meaning of an indeterminate status are solver-interface conventions requiring a specific standard or solver reference.

children.title: Near-Feasibility Status Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Ambiguous outcomes near primal or dual feasibility boundaries.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Uncertainty Ball with Opposite Feasibility Statuses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp one-dimensional example of bounded-error feasibility ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x=t\), \(x\in\mathbb R_+\), with nominal datum \(\widehat t=0\) and error bound \(|t-\widehat t|\le\delta\), where \(\delta>0\). The admissible value \(t=\delta/2\) gives a feasible system, while \(t=-\delta/2\) gives an infeasible system. Thus the same observation is compatible with opposite exact feasibility statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive uncertainty radius around the scalar boundary at zero contains both a feasible and an infeasible instance.
assumptions_latex: Only \(\widehat t=0\) and the deterministic bound \(|t|\le\delta\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\delta>0\), the admissible data contain both exact feasibility statuses.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Uncertainty Ball with Opposite Feasibility Statuses

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic data-uncertainty formulation of ambiguity near a declared primal or dual feasibility boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a normed data space, a declared feasibility-status map \(S\), a nominal datum \(\widehat D\), and a deterministic uncertainty radius \(\delta\ge0\). The observation \((\widehat D,\delta)\) is status-ambiguous when there exist \(D_1,D_2\) with \(\|D_i-\widehat D\|\le\delta\) and \(S(D_1)\ne S(D_2)\). From this observation alone, no classifier can determine which of those exact statuses belongs to the unknown datum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-error observation is feasibility-status ambiguous when its uncertainty ball contains exact instances with different declared statuses.
assumptions_latex: The status map, data norm, admissible perturbations, and deterministic bounded-error information model are fixed.
No auxiliary exact information beyond \((\widehat D,\delta)\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Opposite statuses within the same uncertainty ball are not identifiable from the nominal datum and radius alone.
review_flags: The nonidentifiability conclusion is relative to the explicitly stated information model.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Error Feasibility-Status Ambiguity

assumptions_latex: Problem data \(D\) are measured in a fixed norm, and statuses are assigned to exact perturbed data.
For some \(\delta>0\), there exist perturbations \(E_f,E_i\) with \(\|E_f\|,\|E_i\|\le\delta\) such that \(D+E_f\) is feasible and \(D+E_i\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No method using data known only within error \(\delta\) can determine the exact feasibility status of \(D\) from those data alone.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: indistinguishable perturbations with opposite exact statuses imply classification ambiguity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary created by data uncertainty near the feasibility-status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The data \(D\) are \(\delta\)-status-ambiguous when the uncertainty ball \(\{D+E:\|E\|\le\delta\}\) intersects both the feasible-data set and the infeasible-data set. Equivalently, there are admissible \(E_f\) and \(E_i\) giving opposite exact statuses. Consequently, observations resolving the data only to radius \(\delta\) cannot distinguish these two possibilities without additional structural information or a smaller uncertainty bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility is ambiguous at precision delta when the admissible data ball contains both feasible and infeasible conic instances.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Feasibility Status Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uncertainty-ball definition is coherent, but the impossibility conclusion depends on the observation and information model. An authoritative condition-analysis source is required before fixing that conclusion.

children.title: Certificate Sensitivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Status changes caused by small perturbations in certificate data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalized Certificate Residual and Sign Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary fixed-cone perturbation bounds for a normalized dual-infeasibility direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\in K\), \(\|d\|=1\), \(Ad=0\), and \(\langle c,d\rangle=-\gamma<0\). With the cone fixed and data changed to \(A+\Delta A\) and \(c+\Delta c\), \[\|(A+\Delta A)d\|\le\|\Delta A\|,\qquad \langle c+\Delta c,d\rangle\le-\gamma+\|\Delta c\|_*.\] Thus \(\|\Delta c\|_*<\gamma\) preserves the strict sign, whereas exact certificate validity additionally requires \(\Delta A d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a normalized certificate direction, objective perturbations smaller than its strict margin preserve the sign, while generic operator perturbations destroy the exact nullspace equation even when their residual is small.
assumptions_latex: The cone and norm are fixed; only \(A\) and \(c\) are perturbed.
\(\|\Delta A\|\) is the induced operator norm and \(\|\Delta c\|_*\) the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\Delta c\|_*<\gamma\) preserves the negative sign, while exact nullspace feasibility is preserved exactly when \(\Delta A d=0\).

notation.meaning: Dual norm corresponding to the normalization norm.

review_flags: This is a fixed-direction, fixed-cone perturbation bound, not a condition-number theorem.
A small equality residual is numerical evidence only; it does not preserve exact validity.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Certificate Residual and Sign Sensitivity

assumptions_latex: A normalized dual-infeasibility ray satisfies \(d\in K\), \(\|d\|=1\), \(Ad=0\), and \(\langle c,d\rangle=-\gamma<0\).
Data are perturbed to \(A+\Delta A\) and \(c+\Delta c\), with the cone unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign test remains strict when \(\|\Delta c\|_*<\gamma\), while the equality defect is at most \(\|\Delta A\|\); robustness is governed by these defects relative to \(\gamma\).

notation.meaning: Dual norm corresponding to the ray norm.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct norm-margin perturbation estimate for an alternative-system certificate
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise sensitivity of a normalized dual-infeasibility certificate with fixed cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the perturbation, \[\|(A+\Delta A)d\|\le\|\Delta A\|,\qquad \langle c+\Delta c,d\rangle\le-\gamma+\|\Delta c\|_*.\] Hence \(\|\Delta c\|_*<\gamma\) preserves the strict negative sign. The certificate is robust when its margin \(\gamma\) dominates objective-data error and its equality defect is below the validation threshold; it is sensitive when either quantity is comparable to the corresponding error scale. Exact validity additionally requires restoration of the homogeneous equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate robustness is controlled by its strict sign margin and homogeneous-equation defect relative to objective and operator perturbations.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Sensitivity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed norm estimates are plausible under induced operator norms, but the robustness regime and validation-threshold interpretation lack a cited sensitivity source and a fully specified perturbation model.

children.title: Finite-Precision Classification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on robust status discrimination under numerical error.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-neutral control rule when certified diagnostic enclosures meet a classification boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute certified enclosures for every diagnostic defining a proposed status. Return that status only when every enclosure lies wholly in its required acceptance region. Otherwise refine the arithmetic or data bounds and recompute; if separation is not obtained under the permitted refinement, return indeterminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify only after rigorous interval separation; otherwise refine precision or return indeterminate.
assumptions_latex: Every enclosure contains the corresponding exact diagnostic value.
A status requires simultaneous validation of all its defining predicates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No status is returned solely from an enclosure intersecting one of its acceptance boundaries.
review_flags: No finite-termination guarantee is asserted when an exact diagnostic is on or arbitrarily near a boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Validated Classification with Precision Escalation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient interval conditions for validating residual and strict-sign predicates in finite precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the exact residual \(r\) and sign margin \(\gamma\) satisfy \(\|r\|\le \|\widehat r\|+\eta_r\) and \(\gamma\ge \widehat\gamma-\eta_\gamma\), where the nonnegative \(\eta_r,\eta_\gamma\) are certified error bounds. Then \[\|\widehat r\|+\eta_r\le\varepsilon_r,\qquad \widehat\gamma-\eta_\gamma>0\] certify \(\|r\|\le\varepsilon_r\) and \(\gamma>0\). Failure of either sufficient inequality certifies neither acceptance nor rejection from these enclosures alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical predicate is certified when its entire rigorous error enclosure lies on the accepting side of every threshold; overlap merely withholds certification.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta_r\) and \(\eta_\gamma\) rigorously cover the declared data and arithmetic errors.
The norm and acceptance thresholds are fixed before classification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed separated-enclosure inequalities imply both exact acceptance predicates.
review_flags: Failure of this sufficient test does not establish that values on both sides of a threshold are attainable.
knowledge_statements.title: Certified Separation from Classification Thresholds

assumptions_latex: Computed data and candidate certificates carry certified error bounds in a fixed norm.
A classifier accepts statuses using residual thresholds and strict-sign margins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Classification is certified only when error intervals lie wholly inside one status predicate; overlap with a predicate boundary requires an indeterminate result.

notation.meaning: Computed strict-sign margin and its error bound.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: interval separation is necessary for certified finite-precision predicate evaluation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval-based boundary for reliable finite-precision status classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the exact residual and margin obey \(\|r\|\le\|\widehat r\|+\eta_r\) and \(\gamma\ge\widehat\gamma-\eta_\gamma\), then a tolerance test \(\|r\|\le\varepsilon_r\), \(\gamma>0\) is certified only if \[\|\widehat r\|+\eta_r\le\varepsilon_r,\qquad \widehat\gamma-\eta_\gamma>0.\] If either interval intersects its acceptance boundary, rounding-consistent exact quantities can produce different classifications; the finite-precision result must therefore remain indeterminate or be recomputed more accurately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-precision status is reliable only when certified error intervals remain strictly inside every residual and sign acceptance boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Classification Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sufficient interval-separation test is plausible, but overlap of a conservative enclosure with a boundary does not alone prove that both classifications are attainable. A numerical-certification source and precise enclosure assumptions are needed.

children.title: Maximal-Complementarity Variable Partition
children.top_down_role: Embedding-based identification of optimal partitions and limiting variable roles.

children.title: Maximally Complementary Solution Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovery of solutions representing relative interiors of optimal faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximally Complementary Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite recovery criterion based on relative interiors of the primal optimal set and dual optimal-slack set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recovered optimal pair \((X^*,S^*)\) is maximally complementary when \(X^*\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal X^*)\) and \(S^*\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal S^*)\). Such matrices have maximal rank within their respective optimal sets, and their support subspaces represent the maximal primal and dual optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior primal and dual optimal solutions have maximal ranks within their optimal sets and represent the maximal complementary optimal faces.
assumptions_latex: A primal-dual semidefinite program attains a common finite optimal value.
The nonempty set of primal optimal matrices is \(\mathcal X^*\), and the nonempty set of dual optimal slack matrices is \(\mathcal S^*\).
Relative interiors are taken in the affine hulls of \(\mathcal X^*\) and \(\mathcal S^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any pair \((X^*,S^*)\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal X^*)\times\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal S^*)\) is maximally complementary and represents the maximal primal and dual optimal faces.

notation.meaning: Primal optimal matrix set and dual optimal-slack matrix set.
Relative interior in the affine hull.
Recovered primal optimal matrix and dual optimal slack matrix.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X^*\) and \(\mathcal S^*\) are nonempty convex optimal sets in finite-dimensional spaces.
For each optimal set, a finite family of its points has affine hull equal to the affine hull of that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar X\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal X^*)\) and \(\bar S\in\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal S^*)\), so \((\bar X,\bar S)\) is maximally complementary.

notation.meaning: Strictly positive averaging weights summing to one.
Recovered primal optimum and dual optimal slack.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional construction of relative-interior optimal solutions from affine-hull-spanning optimal families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional vector space, and let \(z_0,\ldots,z_m\in C\) satisfy \(\operatorname{aff}\{z_0,\ldots,z_m\}=\operatorname{aff}C\). If \(\lambda_i>0\) and \(\sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i=1\), then \(\bar z=\sum_{i=0}^m\lambda_i z_i\in\operatorname{ri}C\). Applying this construction separately to affine-hull-spanning families in \(\mathcal X^*\) and \(\mathcal S^*\) recovers a pair in \(\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal X^*)\times\operatorname{ri}(\mathcal S^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly positive average of optimal points spanning an optimal set's affine hull lies in its relative interior; applying this to both optimal sets recovers a maximally complementary pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Recovery by Affine-Hull Averaging

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is regarded in its affine hull.
The set \(C\) can occur as the optimal set of an SDP, for example by imposing the displayed diagonal affine form, \(0\le t\le1\), and a constant objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}X=\max_{Z\in C}\operatorname{rank}Z\not\Rightarrow X\in\operatorname{ri}C\).

notation.meaning: A line segment of positive-semidefinite diagonal matrices realizable as an SDP optimal set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of rank-only testing for relative-interior membership in an SDP optimal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{\operatorname{diag}(1,t):0\le t\le1\}\subseteq\mathbb S_+^2\). Every \(\operatorname{diag}(1,t)\) with \(t>0\) has the maximum rank two attained in \(C\), but \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1)\notin\operatorname{ri}C=\{\operatorname{diag}(1,t):0<t<1\}\). Thus maximum rank is necessary but not sufficient for relative-interior membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum-rank optimal matrix can lie on the relative boundary of its optimal set, so rank alone does not certify maximally complementary recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximal Rank Alone Does Not Certify Relative-Interior Recovery
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Rank Alone Does Not Certify Relative-Interior Recovery

children.title: Small–Large Variable Separation
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic partitioning of complementary variables.

assumptions_latex: A primal-dual semidefinite central sequence \((X(\mu),S(\mu))\) satisfies \(X(\mu)S(\mu)=\mu I\) for \(\mu>0\).
The sequence converges to a maximally complementary optimal pair \((X^*,S^*)\) with complementary support subspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eigenvalues associated with the support of \(X^*\) stay large while their complementary slack eigenvalues are \(O(\mu)\), and conversely on the support of \(S^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic eigenvalue separation along a semidefinite central sequence.

source_refs.locator: 5.7 Separating small and large variables p. 128

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On any limiting eigenspace where \(X^*\) is positive definite, the corresponding eigenvalues of \(X(\mu)\) are bounded below away from zero, and complementarity forces the paired eigenvalues of \(S(\mu)\) to be \(O(\mu)\). On the complementary support where \(S^*\) is positive definite, the roles reverse. Thus, for sufficiently small \(\mu\), a threshold strictly between the \(O(\mu)\) scale and the positive limiting scale recovers the maximal complementary support partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a central sequence, eigenvalues split into positive-limit large values and complementary order-mu small values, revealing the maximal support partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Small–Large Variable Separation

source_witnesses.locator: 5.7 Separating small and large variables p. 128

assumptions_latex: The central sequence satisfies the seed assumptions, including \(X(\mu)S(\mu)=\mu I\) and convergence to a maximally complementary pair.
For small \(\mu\), every small-group eigenvalue is at most \(C\mu\), and every large-group eigenvalue is at least \(\delta>0\), for constants \(C\) and \(\delta\) independent of \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any threshold satisfying \(C\mu<\theta(\mu)<\delta\) correctly separates the two groups; without a uniform positive \(\delta\), scale-based threshold recovery is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: Eigenvalue threshold used for support classification.
Uniform upper-bound constant for small eigenvalues and positive lower bound for large eigenvalues.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform spectral-gap condition and its failure boundary for support classification along a semidefinite central sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the small eigenvalues are bounded above by \(C\mu\) and the large eigenvalues are bounded below by \(\delta>0\), uniformly for all sufficiently small \(\mu\). Then every threshold \(\theta(\mu)\) satisfying \(C\mu<\theta(\mu)<\delta\) recovers the small-large partition. Equivalently, an asymptotic choice with \(\mu=o(\theta(\mu))\) and \(\theta(\mu)=o(1)\) works under these uniform bounds. If the purported large eigenvalues have no positive uniform lower bound, no threshold justified solely by an \(O(\mu)\)-versus-positive-limit split is guaranteed to recover the maximal optimal support partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Threshold recovery requires a uniform gap between order-mu eigenvalues and eigenvalues bounded away from zero; without that gap, the support partition is not uniformly identifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform Spectral Gap for Small-Large Separation
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Spectral Gap for Small-Large Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Central-Path Bounds Separating the Embedding Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative separation of the embedding variables along the positive-parameter path in the two maximally complementary regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\mu>0\), where \((\tau^*,\rho^*)\) denotes the corresponding components of a maximally complementary solution,
\[
\tau^*>0,\ \rho^*=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\tau(\mu)\ge \frac{\sigma}{\widetilde n},\qquad
\rho(\mu)\le \frac{\widetilde n\mu}{\sigma},
\]
and
\[
\tau^*=0,\ \rho^*>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\tau(\mu)\le \frac{\widetilde n\mu}{\sigma},\qquad
\rho(\mu)\ge \frac{\sigma}{\widetilde n}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive path parameter, the variable whose maximally complementary limit is positive stays at least sigma divided by the embedding dimension, while the variable whose limit is zero is at most the embedding dimension times mu divided by sigma. The roles reverse in the opposite maximally complementary regime.
assumptions_latex: (\tau^*,\rho^*)\text{ are components of a maximally complementary solution}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\tau^*>0,\rho^*=0)\Rightarrow\left(\tau(\mu)\ge\frac{\sigma}{\widetilde n},\ \rho(\mu)\le\frac{\widetilde n\mu}{\sigma}\right),\quad (\tau^*=0,\rho^*>0)\Rightarrow\left(\tau(\mu)\le\frac{\widetilde n\mu}{\sigma},\ \rho(\mu)\ge\frac{\sigma}{\widetilde n}\right)

source_evidence.locator: Self-Dual Embeddings / 5.7. Separating small and large variables / Lemma 5.7.1

source_refs.locator: Self-Dual Embeddings / 5.7. Separating small and large variables / Lemma 5.7.1

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Path Bounds Separating the Embedding Variables

source_witnesses.locator: Self-Dual Embeddings / 5.7. Separating small and large variables / Lemma 5.7.1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood Bounds for Small–Large Embedding Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-iterate separation bounds for a feasible embedding point lying in a bounded centrality neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\widetilde X,\widetilde S)\) be feasible for the embedding problem and suppose \(\delta(\widetilde X,\widetilde S)\le\kappa\) for some \(\kappa>1\). If \((\tau^*,\rho^*)\) denotes the corresponding components of a maximally complementary solution, then
\[
\tau^*>0,\ \rho^*=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\tau\ge\frac{\sigma}{\kappa n},\qquad
\rho\le\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\bar X\bar S)}{\sigma},
\]
and
\[
\tau^*=0,\ \rho^*>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\tau\le\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(\bar X\bar S)}{\sigma},\qquad
\rho\ge\frac{\sigma}{\kappa n}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At any feasible embedding point whose centrality measure is at most kappa greater than one, the variable positive in a maximally complementary solution is bounded below by sigma divided by kappa n, while the variable vanishing there is bounded above by the complementarity trace divided by sigma. The bounds reverse with the complementary regime.
assumptions_latex: (\widetilde X,\widetilde S)\text{ is feasible for the embedding problem}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\delta>0\) denote the required relative accuracy. If each iteration of \(S_N(R)\) has arithmetic complexity \(O\!\left(n^2(n+p)\right)\), then the total arithmetic complexity of method \((7.1.30)\) is bounded by
\[
O\!\left(n^2p^2+\frac{1}{\delta}n^{5/2}(p+n)\ln n\right).
\]
The worst-case arithmetic complexity of a short-step path-following scheme applied to problems \((7.1.20)\)–\((7.1.37)\) is
\[
O\!\left(pn^{5/2}(p+n)\ln\frac{n}{\delta}\right).
\]
According to the proposition's asymptotic comparison, the gradient-type method is preferable when the required relative accuracy is not too small, for example when \(\delta\) is at least of order \(p^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each iteration of S_N(R) costs on the order of n squared times n plus p arithmetic operations, method (7.1.30) uses at most on the order of n squared p squared plus delta inverse times n to the five-halves times p plus n times log n operations. A short-step path-following scheme for the referenced problems has worst-case arithmetic complexity on the order of p times n to the five-halves times p plus n times log(n/delta). The proposition's asymptotic comparison favors the gradient-type method when the requested relative accuracy is not too small, for example when delta is at least of order 1/p.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Embedded Residual without Stable Dehomogenization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination boundary showing why embedded convergence must control the homogenizing scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a homogeneous embedding reports \(r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}\) and recovery gives \(r_k^{\mathrm{rec}}=r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}/\tau_k\) for \(\tau_k>0\). Let \(\tau_k=2^{-k}\) and \(\|r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}\|=2^{-k/2}\). Then \(\|r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}\|\to0\), but \[\|r_k^{\mathrm{rec}}\|=2^{k/2}\to\infty.\] Therefore an absolute augmented-residual stopping rule cannot ensure decoded accuracy unless it also controls \(\tau_k\) or the normalized residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedded residual may vanish while its decoded residual diverges when the homogenizing scale vanishes faster.
assumptions_latex: The selected embedding recovers the original residual by division by \(\tau_k>0\).
Termination observes only the absolute embedded residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}\to0\ \centernot\Longrightarrow\ r_k^{\mathrm{emb}}/\tau_k\to0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-independent obstruction to transferring embedding accuracy through dehomogenization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let r_j\ge0 and \tau_j>0, with decoded residual \widehat r_j=r_j/\tau_j. Embedded convergence r_j\to0 does not imply \widehat r_j\to0 when \tau_j\to0; for example, r_j=\tau_j=1/j gives \widehat r_j=1. Transfer is ensured by \inf_j\tau_j>0, or more generally by r_j=o(\tau_j).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone, let \((x_k,s_k)\in\operatorname{int}K\times\operatorname{int}K^*\) be the primal-dual iterate at index \(k\), and let \(\Phi_k=\Phi(x_k,s_k)\) be a joint potential. Fix \(\Phi_{\rm tar}\in\mathbb{R}\), and define the target set by \(\Phi(x,s)\leq\Phi_{\rm tar}\). Suppose every accepted update made outside the target set satisfies \[\Phi_{k+1}\leq\Phi_k-\gamma\] for a constant \(\gamma>0\). Then the method enters the target set within at most \[\max\!\left\{0,\left\lceil\frac{\Phi_0-\Phi_{\rm tar}}{\gamma}\right\rceil\right\}\] accepted steps. A residual or duality-gap complexity bound additionally requires a specified potential threshold that implies the requested accuracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iteration bound from uniform primal-dual potential decrease
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connects a fixed per-iteration decrease of the symmetric-cone primal-dual potential to an objective-gap complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\) be a Euclidean Jordan algebra of rank \(r\), set \(q=r+\sqrt r\), and let \((x_0,y_0,s_0)\) be an interior primal-dual feasible point with \(s_0=c-A^Ty_0\). Suppose
\[
\psi(x_0,s_0)\le O(\sqrt r\,E)
\]
for a constant \(E\), and an algorithm produces interior primal-dual feasible iterates satisfying, for some fixed \(\delta>0\),
\[
\psi(x_j,s_j)\ge \psi(x_{j+1},s_{j+1})+\delta.
\]
Then, for every \(\epsilon>0\), after
\[
k=O\!\left(\sqrt r\,(E+|\log\epsilon|)\right)
\]
iterations,
\[
\langle c,x_k\rangle-b^Ty_k<\epsilon.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a rank-r symmetric cone, an interior primal-dual algorithm whose potential starts at order square-root-r times E and decreases by a fixed positive amount each iteration reaches primal-dual objective gap below epsilon in order square-root-r times E plus the absolute logarithm of epsilon iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k=O\!\left(\sqrt r\,(E+|\log\epsilon|)\right)\Longrightarrow \langle c,x_k\rangle-b^Ty_k<\epsilon

Outside the \(\varepsilon\)-target set, each accepted step decreases \(\Phi_L\) by at least \(\gamma_L>0\).
The target threshold satisfies \(\Phi_{L,\rm tar}=a+b\log(1/\varepsilon)\) for fixed scaling constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted-step count is at most \(\lceil(Phi_L(z_0)-Phi_{L,\rm tar})/gamma_L\rceil\) whenever the numerator is positive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional decrement bound; the taxonomy does not identify a unique linear scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_k\) denote an interior primal-dual iterate and let \(\Phi_L(z_k)\) be the potential associated with a specified linear scaling. Suppose the \(\varepsilon\)-target set is characterized by \(\Phi_L(z)leq\Phi_{L,\rm tar}\), where \(\Phi_{L,\rm tar}=a+b\log(1/\varepsilon)\), and every accepted step outside that set satisfies \(\Phi_L(z_{k+1})leq\Phi_L(z_k)-\gamma_L\) for \(\gamma_L>0\). Then the method enters the target set after at most \[left\lceil\frac{\Phi_L(z_0)-Phi_{L,\rm tar}}{\gamma_L}\right\rceil\] accepted steps, with zero steps required when the initial potential already meets the threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed linear scaling, complexity is the initial excess potential divided by the guaranteed per-step potential decrease.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Scaling Potential Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement and conclusion contain malformed TeX, including unescaped `Phi`, `gamma`, `left`, and `leq`. More fundamentally, neither the linear scaling nor its potential is defined, and no source supports the asserted logarithmic target threshold or its inequality direction. Those choices determine the mathematical claim, so an authoritative scaling-specific source is required.

children.title: Projective-Scaling Potential Complexity
children.top_down_role: Potential-reduction complexity associated with projective-scaling formulations.

assumptions_latex: A projectively invariant potential \(\Phi_P\) is defined on rays of interior embedding points.
The stopping set is represented by \(\Phi_P\leq\Phi_{P,\rm tar}(\varepsilon)\).
Every accepted projective-scaling step decreases \(\Phi_P\) by at least \(\gamma_P>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted-step count is at most \(\lceil(Phi_P([z_0])-Phi_{P,\rm tar}(varepsilon))/\gamma_P\rceil\) when positive.

notation.meaning: ray represented by a nonzero embedding point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional ray-invariant decrement bound; exact projective scaling is unresolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonzero interior embedding points be identified by \(z\sim	t z\) for \(t>0\), and let \(Phi_P([z])\) be a well-defined potential on the resulting rays. Suppose the \(varepsilon\)-target set is \(\Phi_P([z])leq\Phi_{P,\rm tar}(varepsilon)\), and every accepted projective-scaling step outside it satisfies \(\Phi_P([z_{k+1}])leq\Phi_P([z_k])-gamma_P\), where \(\gamma_P>0\). Then the target is reached within \[left\lceil\frac{\Phi_P([z_0])-Phi_{P,\rm tar}(varepsilon)}{\gamma_P}\right\rceil\] accepted steps whenever the numerator is positive. The bound is unchanged by positive rescaling of any representative \(z_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projectively invariant potential yields a representative-independent iteration bound from its initial excess and guaranteed decrement.
knowledge_statements.title: Projective-Scaling Potential Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement contains malformed TeX, including `\sim\tt`, unescaped `Phi`, `varepsilon`, `leq`, `gamma`, and `left`. The projective embedding, ray space, invariant potential, stopping threshold, and decrement theorem are also unspecified and uncited. A projective-scaling-specific authoritative source is necessary before the complexity statement can be repaired reliably.

children.title: Comparative Potential-Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural complexity tradeoffs between the alternative scaling families.

assumptions_latex: Two potential-reduction methods start from the same point \(z_0\) and terminate when \(\Phi_i(z)\le \tau_i\).
Each accepted iteration of method \(i\) decreases \(\Phi_i\) by at least \(\delta_i>0\).
On the common trajectory region, \(\lvert \Phi_1(z)-a\Phi_2(z)\rvert\le C\) for constants \(a>0\) and \(C\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_i\le \left\lceil(\Phi_i(z_0)-\tau_i)_+/\delta_i\right\rceil\), with cross-scaling comparisons obtained from the bounded discrepancy \(C\).

notation.meaning: potential used by scaling regime i
guaranteed potential decrease per accepted iteration

review_flags: Exact linear-versus-projective potential comparison requires a dedicated source and normalization convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract comparison for potential functions related by positive rescaling and bounded additive discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i\in\{1,2\}\), let method \(i\) stop at the first iterate satisfying \(\Phi_i(z)le\tau_i\). If every preceding accepted step satisfies \(\Phi_i(z^{k+1})\le\Phi_i(z^k)-\delta_i\), then
\[
N_i\le \left\lceil\frac{(\Phi_i(z_0)-\tau_i)_+}{\delta_i}\right\rceil.
\]
If additionally \(\lvert\Phi_1(z)-a\Phi_2(z)\rvert\le C\) throughout the common region, then \(\Phi_1(z_0)-\tau_1\le a\Phi_2(z_0)+C-\tau_1\). Thus alternative scaling changes the iteration estimate only through the potential normalization, decrement constant, stopping threshold, and bounded discrepancy; no scaling-independent ordering follows without comparing those quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundedly equivalent potentials yield comparable iteration estimates after accounting for normalization, guaranteed decrease, stopping threshold, and additive discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.title: Comparative Potential-Scaling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a generic descent-counting observation rather than a sourced comparison of linear-, projective-, or alternative-scaling potential regimes. The bounded-discrepancy premise does not by itself establish a two-sided comparison of iteration counts, and the statement contains malformed TeX such as `le`.

children.title: Inexact Interior-Point Complexity
children.top_down_role: Convergence with approximate Newton systems and barrier oracles.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Polynomial-Time Interior-Point Method for Conic Optimization, With Inexact Barrier Evaluations
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Polynomial-Time Interior-Point Method for Conic Optimization, With Inexact Barrier Evaluations

children.title: Inexact Newton-Direction Complexity
children.top_down_role: Convergence regimes for approximate linear-system solutions.

assumptions_latex: The cone admits a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier, and the exact short-step method remains in a fixed central neighborhood.
At iteration \(k\), the approximate Newton direction satisfies \(\lVert\widetilde\Delta_k-Delta_k\rVert_{H_k}le\eta\lVert\Delta_k\rVert_{H_k}\) for a uniform sufficiently small \(\eta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon)=O\!\left(\sqrt{\nu}\log(\nu\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right)\), with a constant depending on the neighborhood and \(\eta\).
review_flags: A source is required for the admissible relative-error threshold and neighborhood-dependent constants.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Short-step path following with uniformly controlled error in the local barrier metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider short-step path following for a conic problem with a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier. Let \(\Delta_k\) be the exact Newton direction and \(\widetilde\Delta_k\) the computed direction. If a fixed central neighborhood is maintained and
\[
\lVert\widetilde\Delta_k-Delta_k\rVert_{H_k}le\eta\lVert\Delta_k\rVert_{H_k}
\]
holds for every iteration with \(\eta\) below a neighborhood-dependent constant, then the barrier parameter can be reduced by a factor \(1-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\nu})\) per iteration. Consequently, reaching duality gap at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(O(\sqrt{\nu}\log(\nu\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) iterations; only the hidden constant changes with \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly accurate approximate Newton directions preserve short-step iteration order, although constants depend on the error tolerance and central neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Newton-Direction Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A dedicated inexact interior-point theorem is required. The stated direction-error condition does not specify the primal-dual formulation, neighborhood, local norm, update rule, or admissible error threshold sufficiently to support the claimed complexity bound. Several TeX relations are also malformed.

children.title: Inexact Barrier-Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Convergence regimes for approximate barrier derivative evaluations.

assumptions_latex: The exact barrier \(F\) is \(\nu\)-self-concordant on the cone interior.
Approximate derivatives satisfy uniform local relative-error bounds with sufficiently small constants \(\delta_g,\delta_H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbed short-step scheme has iteration count \(O\!\left(\sqrt{\nu}\log(\nu\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right)\).
review_flags: A dedicated inexact-oracle theorem is needed to fix admissible errors and neighborhood constants.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative local-norm errors in both barrier gradient and Hessian evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H(x)=\nabla^2F(x)\). Suppose the oracle returns \(\widetilde g(x)\) and \(\widetilde H(x)\) such that, at every queried interior point,
\[
\lVert\widetilde g(x)-\nabla F(x)\rVert_{H(x)^{-1}}le\delta_g,
\qquad
(1-delta_H)H(x)\preceq\widetilde H(x)\preceq(1+delta_H)H(x).
\]
If \(\delta_g\) and \(\delta_H\) are uniformly below constants determined by the chosen short-step neighborhood, Newton steps formed from the approximate oracle remain in a slightly enlarged central neighborhood. The resulting method retains the iteration order \(O(\sqrt{\nu}\log(\nu\mu_0/\varepsilon))\), with constants deteriorating as the oracle errors approach their admissible limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small uniform local errors in barrier gradients and Hessians preserve short-step complexity up to changed constants.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Barrier-Oracle Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The admissible gradient and Hessian errors and the mechanism preserving a central neighborhood depend on a precise inexact-oracle model. No source fixes those hypotheses, and malformed expressions such as `le` and `delta_H` make the displayed conditions unreliable.

children.title: Local-Asymptotic Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local rates and active-structure behavior beyond global polynomial iteration theory.

children.title: Local Superlinear Convergence Families
children.top_down_role: Superlinear regimes for suitable predictor-corrector and conic direction families.

assumptions_latex: The primal-dual residual map \(R\) is continuously differentiable near a solution \(z^*\), its Jacobian is locally Lipschitz, and \(R'(z^*)\) is nonsingular.
The computed direction satisfies \(\lVert R'(z_k)d_k+R(z_k)\rVert\le\eta_k\lVert R(z_k)\rVert\) with \(\eta_k\to0\).
Eventually full steps are accepted and the iterates remain in the local conic neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert z_{k+1}-z^*\rVert/\lVert z_k-z^*\rVert\to0\).
review_flags: Conic predictor-corrector specializations and their regularity hypotheses require a dedicated source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local inexact-Newton formulation encompassing regular predictor-corrector direction families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_{k+1}=z_k+d_k\), where \(d_k\) is a predictor-corrector or conic Newton direction satisfying
\[
\lVert R'(z_k)d_k+R(z_k)\rVert\le\eta_k\lVert R(z_k)\rVert,
\qquad \eta_k\to0.
\]
If \(R'\) is locally Lipschitz, \(R'(z^*)\) is nonsingular, \(z_k\to z^*\), and full steps are eventually admissible, then
\[
\frac{\lVert z_{k+1}-z^*\rVert}{\lVert z_k-z^*\rVert}to0.
\]
Hence the family is locally q-superlinear. If the forcing terms additionally satisfy \(\eta_k=O(\lVert R(z_k)\rVert)\), the same regularity assumptions give the quadratic local regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular conic Newton families become locally superlinear when linearization errors vanish relative to the residual and full steps are eventually accepted.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Superlinear Convergence Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a local convergence theorem, not merely a property. Although it resembles a standard inexact-Newton result, a source is needed for its application to conic predictor-corrector families and for the asserted quadratic specialization. The convergence quotient also contains malformed TeX.

children.title: Asymptotic Optimal-Face Identification
children.top_down_role: Limiting identification of active faces and complementary partitions.

assumptions_latex: For a semidefinite primal-dual sequence, \(X_k\to X^*\succeq0\), \(S_k\to S^*\succeq0\), and \(X^*S^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The thresholded ranks stabilize, and the associated spectral projectors converge to the complementary optimal-face subspaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite specialization using thresholded eigenspaces under strict complementarity.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_k^X\) and \(P_k^S\) denote the spectral projectors of \(X_k\) and \(S_k\) onto eigenvalues at least \(\tau_k\). Under convergence, complementarity, strict complementarity, and the stated threshold condition, eventually
\[
\operatorname{rank}P_k^X=operatorname{rank}X^*,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}P_k^S=operatorname{rank}S^*.
\]
Moreover, \(P_k^X\to P_{\operatorname{range}X^*}\) and \(P_k^S\to P_{\operatorname{range}S^*}\), whose ranges are complementary. Thus the minimal primal optimal face and the complementary dual face are identified asymptotically through the limiting spectral partition, although exact finite identification need not occur without thresholding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict complementarity, thresholded eigenspaces eventually recover the dimensions and limiting subspaces of the complementary optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Optimal-Face Identification

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited facial-structure section supports strict complementarity and complementary faces, but the record additionally needs a source for thresholded rank stabilization and spectral-projector convergence. Multiple missing backslashes make the hypotheses and statement malformed, so the exact claim cannot be accepted provisionally.

children.title: Computational Complexity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Separation of iteration counts, per-iteration work, and finite-precision requirements.

children.title: Iteration-Complexity Models
children.top_down_role: Barrier, accuracy, and initialization dependencies of iteration counts.

assumptions_latex: The cone admits a \(\nu\)-self-concordant logarithmically homogeneous barrier.
After an initialization phase of \(N_{\mathrm{init}}\) iterations, a short-step method is in a fixed central neighborhood with complementarity parameter \(\mu_0>0\).
The requested primal-dual gap is at most \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N\le N_{\mathrm{init}}+C\sqrt{\nu}\left\lceil\log\!\left(\frac{\nu\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\right\rceil_+,\] where \(C>0\) depends only on the fixed neighborhood and parameter-update rule.

notation.meaning: complementarity parameter upon entering the central neighborhood
positive part of a real number

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard short-step iteration model with explicit barrier, accuracy, and initialization dependencies.

source_refs.source_title: Linear Matrix Inequalities in System and Control Theory

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The total short-step iteration count is the initialization cost plus a term proportional to the square root of the barrier parameter and the positive part of the logarithm of initial gap scale divided by target accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Iteration-Complexity Models

source_witnesses.source_title: Linear Matrix Inequalities in System and Control Theory

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iteration Count Excludes Work and Precision Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating Newton-step counts from sibling arithmetic and bit-precision models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An iteration bound \(N(\varepsilon)\) counts accepted algorithmic iterations only. It implies neither an arithmetic-operation bound nor a bit-complexity bound unless supplemented respectively by per-iteration work bounds \(W_k\) or finite-precision and encoding-length guarantees. Total arithmetic work is \(\sum_{k=0}^{N(\varepsilon)-1}W_k\), not \(N(\varepsilon)\) alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An iteration count alone does not bound arithmetic work or bit complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(N(\varepsilon)\) bounds the iterations needed to reach tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
\(W_k\) denotes the arithmetic work of iteration \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon)\) alone supplies no bound on \(\sum_{k<N(\varepsilon)}W_k\) or required bit precision.
knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Count Excludes Work and Precision Costs

children.title: Per-Iteration Arithmetic Models
children.top_down_role: Dense, sparse, and structured linear-algebra cost regimes.

assumptions_latex: One Newton iteration factors a dense or sparse symmetric KKT matrix of order \(N\) using a direct factorization.
For the sparse model and a fixed elimination ordering, column \(j\) of the computed triangular factor has \(f_j\) stored entries, including fill.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dense factorization costs \(O(N^3)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(N^2)\) storage, while the sparse factorization costs \(O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^N f_j^2\right)\) arithmetic operations and \(O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^N f_j\right)\) storage.

notation.meaning: order of the Newton or KKT matrix
number of stored entries in factor column j, including fill

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-factorization arithmetic model; cone-block assembly, ordering computation, and iterative-solver costs are excluded.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a direct factorization of a dense symmetric KKT matrix of order \(N\), the leading arithmetic cost per Newton iteration is \(O(N^3)\) and the storage cost is \(O(N^2)\). For a fixed sparse elimination ordering, let \(f_j\) be the number of stored entries in column \(j\) of the computed triangular factor, including fill. The corresponding per-iteration bounds are
\[
O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N} f_j^2\right)\quad\text{arithmetic operations},
\qquad
O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N} f_j\right)\quad\text{storage}.
\]
For \(T\) Newton iterations with the same cost model, the aggregate factorization bounds are obtained by multiplying these quantities by \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense direct KKT factorization has cubic arithmetic cost, whereas sparse direct-factorization cost and storage are governed by fill in the computed factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Per-Iteration Arithmetic Models

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-Newton-step arithmetic and storage model for an iterative KKT or Schur-complement solve; preconditioner-specific convergence rates are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one Newton system is solved in \(q\) iterative-solver iterations. If each iteration uses one operator application costing \(C_{\mathrm{op}}\), one preconditioner application costing \(C_{\mathrm{prec}}\), and \(O(N)\) vector work, while setup costs \(C_{\mathrm{setup}}\), then the arithmetic cost is \[O\!\left(C_{\mathrm{setup}}+q(C_{\mathrm{op}}+C_{\mathrm{prec}}+N)\right).\] If at most \(s\) length-\(N\) work vectors are retained, storage is \(O(S_{\mathrm{op}}+S_{\mathrm{prec}}+sN)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-free Newton solve costs setup plus the solver iteration count times operator, preconditioner, and vector work.
assumptions_latex: The iterative linear solver performs \(q\) iterations during one Newton step.
The stated setup, operator, preconditioner, and workspace quantities include all costs retained by the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=O(C_{\mathrm{setup}}+q(C_{\mathrm{op}}+C_{\mathrm{prec}}+N))\) and \(S=O(S_{\mathrm{op}}+S_{\mathrm{prec}}+sN)\).

notation.meaning: linear-solver iterations in one Newton step
costs of an operator and preconditioner application

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Iterative-Solve Cost Model

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditioning Boundary for Iterative Per-Step Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for replacing direct factorization by an iterative or matrix-free solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Low operator-application cost alone does not imply low Newton-step cost: \(q\) depends on the spectrum, stopping tolerance, and preconditioner. Without a justified bound on \(q\), the matrix-free model gives no dimension-only per-step bound; an insufficient solve tolerance may also fail to produce an admissible interior-point direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cheap matrix-vector products do not guarantee a cheap or admissible Newton step without conditioning and residual control.
assumptions_latex: A Newton system is solved iteratively rather than by exact direct factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without justified bounds on \(q\) and the linear residual, neither a dimension-only step bound nor direction admissibility follows.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Boundary for Iterative Per-Step Costs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense cost of evaluating the structured barrier gradient and Hessian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the arithmetic cost of one gradient-and-Hessian evaluation, not an iteration bound or a total path-following complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the dense model, if evaluating \(g_1,g_2,h_{11},h_{12},h_{22}\) costs \(O(1)\) per index, then the gradient and Hessian of \(F(x,\tau,\xi)\) can be computed in
\[
O(mn^2)
\]
arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With dense data and constant-cost evaluation of each component derivative block, computing both the gradient and Hessian of the structured barrier requires O(m times n squared) arithmetic operations.
assumptions_latex: F\ \text{is the structured barrier under consideration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cost}(\nabla F,\nabla^2F)=O(mn^2)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense Arithmetic Cost of an SDP Newton-Step Subroutine
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-execution arithmetic bound for forming and solving a dense reduced Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m\in\mathbb N\) with \(m\le n(n+1)/2\), and let \(X,U,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Consider the subroutine that forms \(B_j=XA_jX\), assembles \(S\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) and \(d\in\mathbb R^m\) from these matrices and possibly from \(X,U\), solves \(S\lambda=d\), and forms \(\Delta=X[-U+\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(j)}A_j]X\). If matrix multiplication, assembly, the linear solve, and formation of \(\Delta\) use standard dense linear-algebra routines, one execution requires \(O\bigl(n^2(m+n)m\bigr)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard dense arithmetic, one execution of the Newton-step subroutine—forming all X A_j X products, assembling and solving the reduced system, and reconstructing Delta—costs order n squared times m times m plus n arithmetic operations.
assumptions_latex: Matrix multiplication, assembly of \(S,d\), solution of \(S\lambda=d\), and formation of \(\Delta\) use standard dense linear-algebra routines
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cost}=O\bigl(n^2(m+n)m\bigr).\)

children.title: Bit-Precision Complexity Models
children.top_down_role: Encoding-length, numerical-precision, and certification regimes.

children.title: Encoding-Length Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity organization by input encoding length.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Step Count with Exponential Operand Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rational computation showing that iteration count alone does not imply polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \(x_0=2\), perform \(x_{k+1}=x_k^2\). After \(k\) arithmetic steps, \[x_k=2^{2^k},\qquad \ell(x_k)=2^k+O(1).\] Thus \(k\) unit-cost arithmetic steps can produce an operand whose binary encoding length is exponential in \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated squaring uses linearly many arithmetic steps while producing exponentially long exact integers.
assumptions_latex: Squaring is counted as one unit-cost arithmetic operation.
The exact integer is explicitly represented in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T=k,\qquad \ell(x_k)=\Theta(2^k).
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Step Count with Exponential Operand Growth

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Length of Rational Arithmetic Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical size measure for rational operands in a Turing-model computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write a rational number in lowest terms as \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\), \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), taking \(0=0/1\). Up to a fixed convention-dependent additive constant, define \[\ell(a/b)=1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(b+1)\rceil.\] The encoding length of a rational vector, matrix, cone description, iterate, or certificate is the sum of its dimension and structural encodings and its scalar-entry lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational data size is the binary size of reduced numerators and denominators together with dimensions and structural metadata.
assumptions_latex: Rational numbers are stored in reduced binary numerator-denominator form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell(\mathcal D)=\ell(\text{dimensions and structure})+\sum_{q\in\mathcal D}\ell(q).

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of rational quantity q

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Length of Rational Arithmetic Data

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Operand-Size Boundary between Arithmetic and Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounting conditions converting rational arithmetic work into a Turing bit bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a rational algorithm using \(T\) arithmetic and comparison operations. If \(T\) is polynomial in the input and requested output lengths, every operand has polynomial binary length \(S\), and every operation is implemented by an integer-arithmetic routine polynomial in \(S\), then the total bit-operation count is polynomial. A polynomial bound on \(T\) alone gives no such conclusion when operand lengths are unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomially many rational operations imply polynomial bit complexity only when operand sizes and per-operation integer costs are polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: All operands are explicitly encoded rationals.
Arithmetic and comparisons use exact integer routines polynomial in operand length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\leq\operatorname{poly}(L),\ S\leq\operatorname{poly}(L)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{BitCost}\leq\operatorname{poly}(L).

notation.meaning: Number of rational operations and comparisons

knowledge_statements.title: Operand-Size Boundary between Arithmetic and Bit Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model complexity for rational conic input and explicitly encoded approximate output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the total binary length of the rational input, including dimensions and the encoded cone representation, and let \(L_{\mathrm{out}}\) denote the required output-description length, such as \(\lceil\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\rceil\) for absolute accuracy \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). An algorithm has polynomial encoding-length complexity if an instance-independent polynomial \(P\) bounds its number of bit operations, every intermediate encoding length, and its output length by \(P(L+L_{\mathrm{out}})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial encoding-length complexity bounds bit operations and all intermediate and output sizes polynomially in the encoded input and requested output length.
assumptions_latex: Discrete problem data are rational and binary encoded.
The cone description and requested output convention are part of the input specification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{BitCost},\ \max\operatorname{OperandLength},\ \operatorname{OutputLength}\le P(L+L_{\mathrm{out}}).
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Encoding-Length Complexity

assumptions_latex: All discrete input data are rational and represented in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial encoding-length complexity requires polynomial bounds on both the number of bit operations and the bit lengths of intermediate and output quantities as functions of \(L+\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: total binary encoding length of the rational input data

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model definition for rationally encoded conic problem data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) be the total binary encoding length of the rational input, including the dimensions and the encoded cone description, and let \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) be the requested accuracy. An interior-point algorithm has polynomial encoding-length complexity if there is an instance-independent polynomial \(P\) such that it produces an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate encoded output using at most
\[
P\!\left(L+\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\right)
\]
bit operations, while every intermediate and output quantity has encoding length at most the same type of polynomial bound. A polynomial iteration bound alone is insufficient unless the required arithmetic precision, coefficient growth, linear-system computations, and output encoding also obey polynomial bit bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding-length complexity bounds bit operations and the sizes of intermediate and output encodings polynomially in the binary input length and the logarithm of inverse accuracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Length Complexity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Condition-Amplified Sufficient Precision for a Newton Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-error requirement under a declared normwise backward-stability model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=M^{-1}g\). Under the scaled Newton-solve model, if \(\kappa(M)\gamma u<1\), then \[\frac{\|\widehat d-d\|}{\|d\|}\leq\frac{\kappa(M)}{1-\kappa(M)\gamma u}\left(\gamma u+\gamma u\frac{\|g\|}{\|M\|\|d\|}\right)\leq\frac{2\kappa(M)\gamma u}{1-\kappa(M)\gamma u}.\] Therefore, a sufficient condition for relative direction error at most \(\eta\) is \[u\leq\frac{\eta}{\kappa(M)\gamma(2+\eta)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backward-stable Newton solves require condition-dependent precision so that amplified roundoff remains below the allowed direction error.
assumptions_latex: The declared normwise backward-stability model holds.
The same subordinate norm is used throughout.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\leq\eta/[\kappa(M)\gamma(2+\eta)]\Longrightarrow\|\widehat d-d\|/\|d\|\leq\eta.
knowledge_statements.title: Condition-Amplified Sufficient Precision for a Newton Direction

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed Precision Cannot Uniformly Resolve Ill-Conditioned Newton Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal family demonstrating condition-dependent loss of directional accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_t=\operatorname{diag}(1,t)\) and \(g_t=(1,t)^{\mathsf T}\), where \(0<t<1\). The exact solution is \(d=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}\) and \(\kappa_2(M_t)=1/t\). The perturbation \(\Delta g=(0,-t)^{\mathsf T}\) has relative norm tending to zero, but the perturbed solution is \(\widehat d=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\), with relative forward error \(1/\sqrt2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishingly small backward perturbations can cause order-one direction error as the scaled Newton system becomes ill conditioned.
assumptions_latex: Accuracy is judged by Euclidean normwise backward and forward errors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\|\Delta g\|_2}{\|g_t\|_2}\to0,\qquad\frac{\|\widehat d-d\|_2}{\|d\|_2}=1/\sqrt2.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Precision Cannot Uniformly Resolve Ill-Conditioned Newton Systems

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducible normwise finite-precision model for one scaled Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a nonsingular scaled Newton system \(Md=g\), a subordinate norm, and unit roundoff \(u\). A computed direction \(\widehat d\) satisfies a normwise backward-stability model with constant \(\gamma\) if there exist \(\Delta M,\Delta g\) such that \[(M+\Delta M)\widehat d=g+\Delta g,\qquad \|\Delta M\|\leq\gamma u\|M\|,\qquad \|\Delta g\|\leq\gamma u\|g\|.\] The associated condition number is \(\kappa(M)=\|M\|\|M^{-1}\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reproducible precision requirement fixes the scaled system, norm, unit roundoff, backward-error constant, and condition number.
assumptions_latex: The matrix scaling, norm, solver, and arithmetic format are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (M+\Delta M)\widehat d=g+\Delta g\quad\text{with relative perturbations bounded by}\quad\gamma u.

notation.meaning: Condition number in the declared norm

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Newton-Solve Precision Model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Format-independent sufficient condition ensuring that a rounded cone iterate remains strictly interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior, let \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\), and define \(m_K(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial K)\) in a declared norm. If \(\widehat x=x+e\) satisfies \(\|e\|<m_K(x)\), then \(\widehat x\in\operatorname{int}K\). Thus an error bound \(\|e\|\le E(u)\) certifies rounded interiority whenever \(E(u)<m_K(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding preserves strict cone interiority when its certified error is smaller than the iterate's distance to the boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is closed, convex, and has nonempty interior.
Distance and error are measured in the same norm.
The total storage or trial-point error has a certified bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|e\|<\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial K)\Longrightarrow x+e\in\operatorname{int}K.

notation.meaning: Certified arithmetic error bound at unit roundoff u

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Margin Condition for Rounded Interiority

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-agnostic policy for increasing precision when Newton solves or interiority tests cease to be reliable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At working unit roundoff \(u_k\), scale the Newton system, compute a direction using the declared stable solver, and evaluate the prescribed residual, direction-error, and cone-margin bounds. Accept the trial step only when the inexact-Newton tolerance and certified interiority margin hold. Otherwise apply the permitted refinement or regularization at the same precision; if the bounds still fail or stagnate, replace \(u_k\) by a smaller unit roundoff and recompute the factorization. Return numerical failure if the prescribed maximum precision is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the lowest working precision that passes the declared Newton and cone-margin tests, escalating after permitted recovery steps fail.
assumptions_latex: Backward-error and cone-margin estimators are available.
A decreasing sequence of admissible unit roundoffs is declared.
Regularization, refinement, and step-acceptance rules are fixed.
Any regularization bias is included in the acceptance estimator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Every accepted step satisfies the declared inexact-Newton and rounded-interiority tests, or explicit failure is returned.}

notation.meaning: Unit roundoff at precision level k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Precision Growth under a Condition-Number Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mantissa-length requirement when scaled Newton-system conditioning has a known iteration-dependent upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the sufficient direction-accuracy condition \(u_k\leq\eta/[\kappa(M_k)\gamma_k(2+\eta)]\). If \(u_k\leq2^{-p_k}\), \(\kappa(M_k)\leq C\rho_k^{-\alpha}\), and \(\gamma_k\leq\Gamma\), then it suffices to choose \[p_k\geq\left\lceil\log_2\!\left(\frac{C\Gamma(2+\eta)}{\eta}\right)+\alpha\log_2\!\left(\frac1{\rho_k}\right)\right\rceil.\] Thus polynomial condition growth in \(1/\rho_k\) requires only logarithmic mantissa growth in \(1/\rho_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial conditioning envelope yields a mantissa requirement growing logarithmically with inverse path scale.
assumptions_latex: The accepted normwise backward-stability model and direction-error bound apply.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k=O\!\left(\log(C\Gamma/\eta)+\alpha\log(1/\rho_k)\right)\text{ suffices for relative direction error at most }\eta.

notation.meaning: Declared positive path or accuracy scale at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Precision Growth under a Condition-Number Envelope

assumptions_latex: A computed Newton solve has relative residual at most \(c\kappa u+O(u^2)\), where \(u\) is unit roundoff.
The inexact path-following analysis permits relative Newton residual at most \(\eta_{max}<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A sufficient precision condition is \(c\kappa u+O(u^2)\le\eta_{\max}\), equivalently \(p\gtrsim\log_2(c\kappa/\eta_{\max})\) mantissa bits.

notation.meaning: unit roundoff and mantissa length, with u approximately 2 to the minus p
condition number of the scaled Newton system

review_flags: A source is needed for solver-specific backward-error constants and scaling assumptions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient floating-point precision derived from a backward-stable Newton solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a backward-stable linear solver applied to the scaled Newton system produces a relative residual bounded by \(c\kappa u+O(u^2)\), where \(c\) is a dimension- and implementation-dependent stability constant. To satisfy an inexact interior-point requirement of residual at most \(\eta_{\max}\), it is sufficient that
\[
c\kappa u+O(u^2)\le\eta_{\max}.
\]
Ignoring the higher-order term and writing \(u\approx2^{-p}\), a sufficient mantissa length is
\[
p\ge\left\lceil\log_2\!\left(\frac{c\kappa}{\eta_{\max}}\right)\right\rceil.
\]
Consequently, precision must increase when the scaled Newton systems become more ill-conditioned or the admissible inexactness decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Working precision must make condition-number-amplified roundoff smaller than the Newton residual tolerance required by the convergence analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Precision Requirements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is plausible but solver-specific: a backward-error bound does not automatically give the stated forward or relative-residual form `c kappa u`, and the constant can depend on dimension, scaling, factorization, and residual normalization. A numerical linear algebra source and a precise scaled-system model are required.
